#HarryPotter #HarryPotterfanfiction #HarryPotterworldbuilding

The Secretary of Magic and the Rogers Affair

The office of Secretary of Magic is, in formal terms, a cabinet position subject to the same political pressures and constraints as any other. In practice, the authority it confers has grown substantially as the United States expanded from a relatively insulated republic into the preeminent global power. This combination of institutional reach and limited public visibility has periodically attracted candidates whose ambitions or methods proved incompatible with the office.

The most serious case occurred in 1932 with the candidacy of Ezekiel Thomas Rogers. Rogers was of mixed German and Navajo ancestry. He publicly minimized the former while emphasizing a personal narrative of tragedy and self-advancement. His parents, a Navajo father and white mother, were killed on their Arizona farm by a group of Navajo who objected to the couple’s experimentation with Dark Arts—specifically, attempts to combine Aztec blood-magic techniques with contemporary non-magical medical knowledge. Orphaned, Rogers attended Plotinus Academy on scholarship, enlisted in the United States Mage Corps, and was promoted from sergeant to lieutenant for actions against German mages in the First World War. He received the Franklin Star for valor. Throughout this period he continued private research into the Dark Arts his parents had pursued. After the war he obtained papers from an abandoned French magical residence concerning advanced Aztec and Navajo blood practices. He later joined the faculty of the Salem School of Witchcraft as a professor of Ancient Magic Rituals. His 1925 doctoral thesis on a blood-replenishment ritual earned the Galen Prize for Magical Medicine; the work was, in fact, a reconstruction of Aztec rites whose origins he did not disclose.

Around 1930 Rogers completed the Skinwalker transformation. He survived the process by means of Aztec blood-replenishment rituals. Three of the Navajo men responsible for his parents’ deaths did not. Thereafter he required periodic human sacrifices to stabilize his altered state. While cultivating political alliances and standing as a candidate for Secretary of Magic—with the public support of Franklin D. Roosevelt—he grew less able to conceal the physical and mental costs of the transformation.

The disappearance of a young woman last seen in Rogers’s company drew the attention of Freeman Savage, a private investigator and fellow veteran of the First World War. Savage interrupted an attempted sacrifice, extracted the intended victim, and escaped. Rogers responded by having Savage declared a kidnapper and murderer and dispatching Aurors in pursuit. Savage evaded capture, entered the MACUSA building, and, employing a Navajo spell and totem supplied by an associate, revealed Rogers’s nature before the assembled Magical Congress. Rogers resisted; concentrated spellfire together with machine-gun and grenade fire brought him down.

Savage was subsequently recognized as a national hero. President Roosevelt awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom and offered him the post of Secretary of Magic. Savage declined the office but accepted substantial compensation for the resolution of the case. The position then passed to Jonathan Akroyd, a wizard of established reputation who held it through the Second World War.

Savage had many more adventures before, during and after the Second World War... But that's another story.

text:
🧵 The Federalist Papers: 85 essays explaining the American system of government

1/20
In 1787–1788, Hamilton, Madison, and Jay wrote 85 essays urging Americans to ratify the Constitution. Their central question: How do you build a government strong enough to govern but limited enough to preserve liberty?

2/20
Papers 1–14: Unity is strength. Divided states risk trade wars, interstate conflict, foreign manipulation, and military competition. A united republic offers greater security and prosperity.

3/20
Federalist No. 10: Factions are inevitable because people have different interests. The solution isn’t eliminating disagreement, but building a large republic where competing interests make domination harder.

4/20
Papers 15–22: The Articles of Confederation created a national government too weak to enforce its laws or reliably collect revenue. A government that can only ask states for cooperation cannot govern effectively.

5/20
Papers 23–36: National defense and public finances require real federal authority. Congress needs taxation powers, military capacity, and the ability to enforce national laws—but constitutional powers must have legitimate purposes.

6/20
Papers 37–46: The Constitution balances national and state authority. The federal government receives specific powers, while states retain broad responsibilities. Neither level should simply absorb the other.

7/20
Federalist No. 39: America is neither purely national nor merely a league of independent states. Its constitutional system combines popular sovereignty, national authority, and state-based representation.

8/20
Federalist No. 45: The states are not supposed to become administrative departments of Washington. The federal government’s powers are limited and enumerated; state powers cover much of ordinary domestic life.

9/20
Papers 47–51: Power must check power. Separating legislative, executive, and judicial authority is not enough by itself. Each branch needs the institutional means to resist encroachment by the others.

10/20
Federalist No. 51: Government must control the governed, but also control itself. Because people in power are not infallible, constitutional design must account for ambition, self-interest, and human imperfection.

11/20
Papers 52–61: The House of Representatives should remain accountable to voters through frequent elections. Representation must be broad enough to reflect society without becoming too unwieldy to function.

12/20
Papers 62–66: The Senate provides stability, experience, and deliberation. Its role in treaties and impeachment is designed to prevent consequential decisions from resting entirely on temporary political passions.

13/20
Papers 67–77: The presidency needs enough authority to act decisively. But the president is not a king. Elections, limited terms, the veto, Senate confirmation, and constitutional boundaries constrain executive power.

14/20
Federalist No. 70: A single executive promotes energy, decisiveness, and accountability. When responsibility is clear, voters can more easily determine who deserves credit or blame.

15/20
Papers 78–83: The judiciary must remain independent. Courts interpret the law, resolve federal disputes, and protect the Constitution against conflicting legislation. Judges must not simply become instruments of political branches.

16/20
Federalist No. 78: The Constitution is superior to ordinary legislation. When a law conflicts with the Constitution, courts must follow the higher authority rather than the wishes of a temporary legislative majority.

17/20
Federalist No. 84: Hamilton argued that a bill of rights was unnecessary because the federal government possessed only delegated powers. Critics disagreed, and the Bill of Rights was subsequently adopted.

18/20
Federalist No. 85: The Constitution wasn’t presented as perfect. It was presented as the best workable framework available, with amendments possible through the constitutional process.

You're not really engaging with anything I'm saying which is a little frustrating as I've taken quite a lot of time to reply to each of your messages.

Capitalism means something like property and other inputs to production being owned and controlled by businesses and private individuals. That definition can describe a vast span of wildly contrasting realities. What proportion of society’s individuals own these means of production? What size of business? How static is ownership? Are these individuals and businesses foreign or domestic? To what extent are they directed by the states in which they operate? How stable is the model of ownership over time?

The fundamental problems with liberalism and capitalism include inherent instability and excessive vulnerability to capture by hostile, foreign and minority interests. The vulnerability of democracy to extreme corruption was understood as long ago as Plato. We are very far from the ideal form of either liberalism or capitalism. We were probably closest to it in the 19th century when the particular circumstances of the industrial revolution, empire and global naval supremacy were a very large part of the model’s success in Britain. Of course we have none of those things now. Worse, we have lost the social, cultural and moral foundations of this system which we took for granted.

I would return to those conditions in a heartbeat. Nevertheless, we should be honest and admit that life for those at the bottom of society at the peak of our nation’s success was much worse than it had been before urbanisation and industrialization.

But our debate is about what constitutes left and right. The relevance of everything else we’ve been discussing to this question is that the left-right representation reduces every model of human governance to a single vertex on a 1-dimensional axis. In doing so, clearly it is important that this axis measures the most fundamental features of political organisation.

I take issue with your definition of left vs right both because it is an historically inaccurate redefinition and also because it does not measure the most fundamental features of political organisation.

What you want the left-right axis to represent (something like a measure of Isiah Berlin’s negative conception of liberty) is not  fundamental. It is highly desirable but it depends on foundations that are exceedingly rare in human history. They may even have been unique to the Anglosphere for a period of a couple of centuries. Like Chesterton's proverbial fences, we have carelessly and unknowingly ripped away everything that facilitated what might have been the most successful system of government ever developed. Liberty is not the underlying foundation of society. It is something more like a crowning achievement resting on an exceptionally fit body politic.

I don’t want to live in a totalitarian state. For a modern European, still more so an Englishman, it is something that only begins to look like a solution (let alone an ideal) after economic and cultural ruin and facing the prospect of final eradication.That is where Spain and Germany found themselves in the 1930s. It is the destination of our current trajectory in Britain. Far right politics are a REACTION to the far left and foreign subversion. They are not born in a vacuum. They don’t exist in the absence of communist and foreign predation. However much you love liberty and loathe totalitarianism, you are making a mistake to group communism with regimes whose overarching purpose was to defeat communism. There is a very good reason that a synonym for right wing is reactionary.

As with your modified definition of left/right, in your contrast of liberal democracy/capitalism against the 30s German/Spanish regimes, you are again doing what liberals correctly accuse Marxists of doing. Your own ideology is represented in its idealised form. The reality of democracy is that it atrophies as Plato described. Corruption and vast public debt appear unavoidable. Liberal democracy degenerates. The features of society that prevent or arrest its degeneration have been stripped away. Liberalism does this. It was initially (and correctly) understood as progressive and left wing. Unchecked, it is a progressive permanent revolution with no limiting principle. Marx was not wrong in identifying bourgeois liberalism as a step on the path to communism.

The question we have is can we reverse the degeneration and restore something like the better society we had before or will we need something radically different to prevent our descent into communism. The Germans and the Spanish faced a similar dilemma and worse circumstances than our own. Their emergency was so extreme that their solutions were necessarily extreme. It is a communist trap to identify the extreme, last minute measures taken to defeat communism at a point of total ruin as themselves an ultimate evil indistinguishable from communism itself.

You suggest that Hitler was a “raging anti-capitalist”. If you lived in 1930s Germany, you would be too. Hitler was against the actual form of predatory capitalism that had devoured his country, brought about hyper-inflation, mass unemployment, starvation, and made all forms of degeneracy including child prostitution a normal feature of the Weimar Republic. Hitler's antipathy was towards the system of international finance and liberal democracy that destroyed his country's economy and culture. It is understandable. Within the space of a few years, his government brought the country back from total ruin and to affluence and self-confidence. The model (thankfully) has little relevance to contemporary England, except inasmuch as it offers some hope that rapid recovery is possible from worse positions than our own. Then again, it also suggests that such a rescue might make a retaliatory attack all but inevitable.

Returning to the definition of left and right…
You want right and left to represent good and bad.
You either want, or are resigned to, “Nazis” being placed on the bad zone of the spectrum.
As a result you want to group Nazis with Commies and idealised liberalism on the right.

My responses to this conception are really quite simple:

1) this concept of left / right is a corruption of the original and longstanding definition
2) Your re-definition removes the ability to discriminate between the most fundamental differentiators of government models and instead measure against Isiah Berlin's conception of negative freedom.
3) Your model requires reclassifying absolute monarchy, theocracy and feudalism as left wing which is patently absurd.
4) the underlying assumptions that define your model are a one-way ticket to communism, despite this being opposite to your desired outcome. For as long as we accept the cartoonish (and COMMUNIST) framing of the 1930s & 40s German, Spanish & to some extent Italian regimes, we are stuck in a deceitful context-stripped misreading of history that leaves us disarmed in our fight to prevent the circumstances that bring about communism or a last minute rescue from communism by totalitarian right wing government.

text:
Catholic Bold Confessions on the Sabbath Change 

Q. Have you any other proofs that they (Protestants) are not guided by the Scripture?

A. Yes; so many, that we cannot admit more than a mere specimen into this small work. They reject much that is clearly contained in Scripture, and profess more that is nowhere discoverable in that Divine Book.

Q. Give some examples of both?

A. They should, if the Scripture were their only rule, wash the feet of one another, according to the command of Christ, in the 13th chap. of St. John; —they should keep, not the Sunday, but the Saturday, according to the commandment, "Remember thou keep holy the SABBATH-day;" for this commandment has not, in Scripture, been changed or abrogated;... 

—Rev. Stephen Keenan, A Doctrinal Catechism; New York in 1857, page 101 Imprimatuer

They assembled on Saturdays, not that they were infected with Judaism, but only to worship Jesus Christ the Lord of the sabbath —William Cave in his book entitled Primitive Christianity citing Athanasius bishop of Alexandria, pg. 125

It is well to remind the Presbyterians, Baptists, Methodists, and all other Christians, that the Bible does not support them anywhere in their observance of Sunday. Sunday is an institution of the Roman Catholic Church, and those who observe the day observe a commandment of the Catholic Church.

 —Priest Brady, in an address, reported in the Elizabeth, NJ ‘News’ on March 18, 1903.

Protestants ... accept Sunday rather than Saturday as the day for public worship after the Catholic Church made the change... But the Protestant mind does not seem to realize that ... in observing Sunday, they are accepting the authority of the spokesman for the Church, the pope. 

—Our Sunday Visitor, February 5th, 1950.

Of course these two old quotations are exactly correct. The Catholic Church designated Sunday as the day for corporate worship and gets full credit – or blame – for the change. 

—This Rock, The Magazine of Catholic Apologetics and Evangelization, p.8, June 1997

Q. Have you any other way of proving that the Church has power to institute festivals of precept?

A. Had she not such power, she could not have done that in which all modern religionists agree with her; —she could not have substituted the observance of Sunday the first day of the week, for the observance of Saturday the seventh day, a change for which there is no Scriptural authority. 

—Rev. Stephen Keenan, A Doctrinal Catechism; New York in 1857, page 174

Q. In what manner can we show a Protestant, that he speaks unreasonably against fasts and abstinences?

A. Ask him why he keeps Sunday, and not Saturday, as his day of rest, since he is unwilling either to fast or to abstain. If he reply, that the Scripture orders him to keep the Sunday, but says nothing as to fasting and abstinence, tell him the Scripture speaks of Saturday or the Sabbath, but gives no command anywhere regarding Sunday or the first day of the week.

If, then he neglects Saturday as a day of rest and holiness, and substitutes Sunday in its place, and this merely because such was the usage of the ancient Church, should he not, if he wishes to act consistently, observe fasting and abstinence, because the ancient Church so ordained? 

—Rev. Stephen Keenan, A Doctrinal Catechism; New York in 1857, page 181

Question: Which is the Sabbath day?
Answer: Saturday is the Sabbath day.

Question: Why do we observe Sunday instead of Saturday?

Answer: We observe Sunday instead of Saturday because the Catholic Church transferred the solemnity from Saturday to Sunday.

—Rev. Peter Geiermann https://t.co/X4m1ptrA6b.R., The Convert’s Catechism of Catholic Doctrine, p. 50

Q. Must not a sensible Protestant doubt seriously, when he finds that even the Bible is not followed as a rule by his co-religionists?

A. Surely, when he sees them baptize infants, abrogate the Jewish Sabbath, and observe Sunday for which [pg. 7] there is no Scriptural authority; when he finds them neglect to wash one another's feet, which is expressly commanded, and eat blood and things strangled, which are expressly prohibited in Scripture. He must doubt, if he think at all. ...

Q. Should not the Protestant doubt when he finds that he himself holds tradition as a guide?

A. Yes, if he would but reflect that he has nothing but Catholic Tradition for keeping the Sunday holy; ... 

—Controversial Catechism by Stephen Keenan, New Edition, revised by Rev. George Cormack, published in London by Burns & Oates, Limited - New York, Cincinnati, Chicago: Benzinger Brothers, 1896, pages 6, 7.

The Church, on the other hand, after changing the day of rest from the Jewish Sabbath, or seventh day of the week, to the first, made the Third Commandment refer to Sunday as the day to be kept holy as the Lord's Day. 
The Council of Trent (Sess. VI, can. xix) condemns those who deny that the Ten Commandments are binding on Christians.

(The Catholic Encyclopedia, Commandments of God, Volume IV, © 1908 by Robert Appleton Company, Online Edition © 1999 by Kevin Knight, Nihil Obstat - Remy Lafort, Censor Imprimatur - +John M. Farley, Archbishop of New York, page 153.)

The [Roman Catholic] Church changed the observance of the Sabbath to Sunday by right of the divine, infallible authority given to her by her founder, Jesus Christ. The Protestant claiming the Bible to be the only guide of faith, has no warrant for observing Sunday. In this matter the Seventh-day Adventist is the only consistent Protestant. 

—The Catholic Universe Bulletin, August 14, 1942, p. 4.

All of us believe many things in regard to religion that we do not find in the Bible. For example, nowhere in the Bible do we find that Christ or the Apostles ordered that the Sabbath be changed from Saturday to Sunday. We have the commandment of God given to Moses to keep holy the Sabbath Day, that is the 7th day of the week, Saturday. Today most Christians keep Sunday because it has been revealed to us by the Church outside the Bible. 

—The Catholic Virginian, To Tell You The Truth,” Vol. 22, No. 49 (Oct. 3, 1947).

... you may read the Bible from Genesis to Revelation, and you will not find a single line authorizing the sanctification of Sunday. The Scriptures enforce the religious observance of Saturday, a day which we never sanctify.

—The Faith of Our Fathers, by James Cardinal Gibbons, Archbishop of Baltimore, 88th edition, page 89. Originally published in 1876, republished and Copyright 1980 by TAN Books and Publishers, Inc., pages 72-73.

Deny the authority of the Church and you have no adequate or reasonable explanation or justification for the substitution of Sunday for Saturday in the Third - Protestant Fourth - Commandment of God... The Church is above the Bible, and this transference of Sabbath observance is proof of that fact.'

—Catholic Record, September 1, 1923.

But since Saturday, not Sunday, is specified in the Bible, isn't it curious that non-Catholics who profess to take their religion directly from the Bible and not the Church, observe Sunday instead of Saturday? Yes, of course, it is inconsistent; but this change was made about fifteen centuries before Protestantism was born, and by that time the custom was universally observed.

They have continued the custom, even though it rests upon the authority of the Catholic Church and not upon an explicit text in the Bible. That observance remains as a reminder of the Mother Church from which the non-Catholic sects broke away - like a boy running away from home but still carrying in his pocket a picture of his mother or a lock of her hair.

—The Faith of Millions

Perhaps the boldest thing, the most revolutionary change the Church ever did, happened in the first century. The holy day, the Sabbath, was changed from Saturday to Sunday. "The Day of the Lord" (dies Dominica) was chosen, not from any directions noted in the Scriptures, but from the Church's sense of its own power. The day of resurrection, the day of Pentecost, fifty days later, came on the first day of the week. So this would be the new Sabbath. People who think that the Scriptures should be the sole authority, should logically become 7th Day Adventists, and keep Saturday holy.

—Sentinel, Pastor's page, Saint Catherine Catholic Church, Algonac, Michigan, May 21, 1995

If Protestants would follow the Bible, they would worship God on the Sabbath Day. In keeping the Sunday they are following a law of the Catholic Church.

—Albert Smith, Chancellor of the Archdiocese of Baltimore, replying for the Cardinal, in a letter dated February 10, 1920.

The observance of Sunday by the Protestants is homage they pay, in spite of themselves, to the authority of the [Catholic] Church.

—Monsignor Louis Segur, ‘Plain Talk about the Protestantism of Today’, p. 213.

What Important Question Does the Papacy Ask Protestants?

Protestants have repeatedly asked the papacy, "How could you dare to change God's law?" But the question posed to Protestants by the Catholic church is even more penetrating.

Here it is officially: You will tell me that Saturday was the Jewish Sabbath, but that the Christian Sabbath has been changed to Sunday. Changed! but by whom? Who has authority to change an express commandment of Almighty God? When God has spoken and said, Thou shalt keep holy the seventh day, who shall dare to say, Nay, thou mayest work and do all manner of worldly business on the seventh day; but thou shalt keep holy the first day in its stead?

This is a most important question, which I know not how you can answer. You are a Protestant, and you profess to go by the Bible and the Bible only; and yet in so important a matter as the observance of one day in seven as a holy day, you go against the plain letter of the Bible, and put another day in the place of that day which the Bible has commanded.

The command to keep holy the seventh day is one of the ten commandments; you believe that the other nine are still binding; who gave you authority to tamper with the fourth? If you are consistent with your own principles, if you really follow the Bible and the Bible only, you ought to be able to produce some portion of the New Testament in which this fourth commandment is expressly altered.

—Library of Christian Doctrine: Why Don't You Keep Holy the Sabbath-Day? (London: Burns and Oates, Ltd.), pp. 3, 4.

There is but one church on the face of the earth which has the power, or claims power, to make laws binding on the conscience, binding before God, binding under penalty of hell-fire. For instance, the institution of Sunday. What right has any other church to keep this day? You answer by virtue of the third commandment (the papacy did away with the 2nd regarding the worship of graven images, and called the 4th the 3rd), which says 'Remember that thou keep holy the Sabbath day.'

But Sunday is not the Sabbath. Any schoolboy knows that Sunday is the first day of the week. I have repeatedly offered one thousand dollars to anyone who will prove by the Bible alone that Sunday is the day we are bound to keep, and no one has called for the money. It was the holy Catholic Church that changed the day of rest from Saturday, the seventh day, to Sunday, the first day of the week.

—T. Enright, C.S.S.R., in a lecture delivered in 1893.

Of course the Catholic Church claims that the change was her act. And the act is a mark of her ecclesiastical power and authority in religious matters.

—C. F. Thomas, Chancellor of Cardinal Gibbons, in answer to a letter regarding the change of the Sabbath, November 11, 1895.

Tradition, not Scripture, is the rock on which the church of Jesus Christ is built.

—Adrien Nampon, Catholic Doctrine as Defined by the Council of Trent, p. 157

The Pope is of so great authority and power that he can modify, explain, or interpret even divine law". The pope can modify divine law, since his power is not of man, but of God, and he acts a vicegerent of God upon earth.

—Lucius Ferraris, Prompta Bibliotheca, art. Papa, II, Vol. VI, p. 29.

The leader of the Catholic church is defined by the faith as the Vicar of Jesus Christ (and is accepted as such by believers). The Pope is considered the man on earth who "takes the place" of the Second Person of the omnipotent God of the Trinity.

—John Paul II, Crossing the Threshold of Hope, p. 3, 1994

...pastoral intuition suggested to the Church the christianization of the notion of Sunday as "the day of the sun", which was the Roman name for the day and which is retained in some modern languages.(29) This was in order to draw the faithful away from the seduction of cults which worshipped the sun, and to direct the celebration of the day to Christ, humanity's true 'sun'.

—John Paul II, Dies Domini, 27. The day of Christ-Light, 1998 (Prominent protestant leaders agree with this statement - See here for a statement by Dr. E. T. Hiscox, author of the ‘Baptist Manual’)

The Sun was a foremost god with heathen-dom…The sun has worshippers at this hour in Persia and other lands…. There is, in truth, something royal, kingly about the sun, making it a fit emblem of Jesus, the Sun of Justice. Hence the church in these countries would seem to have said, to 'Keep that old pagan name [Sunday]. It shall remain consecrated, sanctified.' And thus the pagan Sunday, dedicated to Balder, became the Christian Sunday, sacred to Jesus.

—William Gildea, Doctor of Divinity, The Catholic World, March, 1894, p. 809
The retention of the old pagan name of Dies Solis, for Sunday is, in a great measure, owing to the union of pagan and Christian sentiment with which the first day of the week was recommended by Constantine to his subjects - pagan and Christian alike - as the 'venerable' day of the sun.

—Arthur P. Stanley, History of the Eastern Church, p. 184

When St. Paul repudiated the works of the law, he was not thinking of the Ten Commandments, which are as unchangeable as God Himself is, which God could not change and still remain the infinitely holy God.

—Our Sunday Visitor, Oct. 7, I951.
Question: How prove you that the Church hath power to command feasts and holydays?

Answer: By the very act of changing the Sabbath into Sunday, which Protestants allow of; and therefore they fondly contradict themselves, by keeping Sunday strictly, and breaking most other feasts commanded by the same Church.

—Henry Tuberville, An Abridgment of the Christian Doctrine (1833 approbation), p.58 (Same statement in Manual of Christian Doctrine, ed. by Daniel Ferris [1916 ed.], p.67)

Some theologians have held that God likewise directly determined the Sunday as the day of worship in the NEW LAW, that he himself has explicitly substituted Sunday for the Sabbath. But this theory is entirely abandoned. It is now commonly held that God simply gave His church the power to set aside whatever day or days she would deem suitable as holy days. The church chose Sunday, the first day of the week, and in the course of time added other days as holy days.

—Vincent J. Kelly, Forbidden Sunday and Feast-Day Occupations, Washington, DC, Catholic University of America Press, Studies in Sacred Theology, No. 70.,1943, p. 2.

If we consulted the Bible only, we should still have to keep holy the Sabbath Day, that is, Saturday, with the Jews, instead of Sunday; ...

—A Course in Religion for Catholic High Schools and Academies, by Rev. John Laux M.A., Benzinger Brothers, 1936 edition, Part 1.

Sunday is a Catholic institution, and... can be defended only on Catholic principles.... From beginning to end of Scripture there is not a single passage that warrants the transfer of weekly public worship from the last day of the week to the first.

—Catholic Press, Aug. 25, 1900

The Sabbath was Saturday, not Sunday. The Church altered the observance of the Sabbath to the observance of Sunday. Protestants must be rather puzzled by the keeping of Sunday when God distinctly said, 'Keep holy the Sabbath Day.' The word Sunday does not come anywhere in the Bible, so, without knowing it they are obeying the authority of the Catholic Church.

—Canon Cafferata, The Catechism Explained, p. 89.

Reason and sense demand the acceptance of one or the other of these alternatives: either Protestantism and the keeping holy of Saturday, or Catholicity and the keeping holy of Sunday. Compromise is impossible.

—John Cardinal Gibbons, The Catholic Mirror, December 23, 1893.

Gad Saad stands as one of the clearest, most uncompromising voices in the defense of truth, reason, and the survival of Western civilization.
He has spent decades applying evolutionary science to expose the suicidal empathy, idea pathogens, and ideological capture that are dismantling open societies. His books, including the #1 New York Times bestseller Suicidal Empathy, his massive public platform, and his willingness to speak where others stay silent have made him both highly respected and a marked target.
In Canada he faced death threats, campus security escorts, locked classrooms, and police advice that he should simply stop saying things that upset people. That environment failed him. He left for the University of Mississippi and the Declaration of Independence Center precisely because the United States still offers something Canada no longer does: the practical capacity to live, speak, and defend oneself.
In Mississippi the local deputies and sheriff have made clear they know his work and will protect him. The Second Amendment is not a slogan there; it is a real deterrent. Tenure, free-speech norms, and the rule of law still function. That combination of institutional respect and physical security is why he is, in practice, as well protected as he is respected.
Mark these words: any attack on Gad Saad—whether physical, professional, or coordinated online—will be treated by a great many people as an attack on all of us who refuse to surrender to the forces he has spent his life documenting. He is not alone. He has a large, loyal audience, and powerful people who understand exactly what his work represents have his back. Those who come for him should understand that the consequences will not be limited to one man.
He has already survived worse than most will ever face. He will continue speaking. And those who value what he defends will not stay silent.

text:
Oct 24, 1942: On a rainy night on Guadalcanal, a sergeant from New Jersey named John Basilone and a handful of machine gunners held their line against a Japanese regiment until dawn. He'd go on to become one of the most famous Marines of World War II.

He was born in 1916, the sixth of ten kids in an Italian immigrant family, and grew up in Raritan, New Jersey. He left school after the eighth grade, caddied at a country club, and drove a laundry truck. At 18 he joined the Army and was sent to the Philippines. He boxed, won a lot, and loved Manila so much his buddies started calling him Manila John.

After his hitch ended he came home and drove a truck again. He was restless. In 1940 he joined the Marines, hoping they'd send him back to Manila. Instead the war came, and in September 1942 he landed on Guadalcanal with the 1st Battalion, 7th Marines, commanded by Lt. Col. Lewis "Chesty" Puller.

The Marines held Henderson Field, the airstrip that was the key to the whole island. In late October the Japanese brought in a fresh division and marched it through the jungle for days to hit the airfield from the south.

On the night of Oct 24, in pouring rain, they came out of the jungle and attacked Puller's battalion, which was stretched thin across more than a mile of front. Basilone was in charge of two sections of heavy water-cooled machine guns, about 15 men, covering a key stretch of the line.

The attacks came in waves all night. The Japanese hit his positions with grenades and mortar fire. One of his gun sections was knocked out, and only two of its men were left standing. Basilone hauled a spare machine gun into position and got it firing. Then he repaired another gun that had jammed and manned it himself, firing until his ammunition ran low, holding the line until reinforcements could get to them.

Ammunition got dangerously short, and the supply line was cut. Basilone took off through the dark, through ground where Japanese soldiers had broken through, and came back with belts of ammunition for his gunners. According to the men who were there, by morning the bodies of Japanese soldiers were piled so high in front of his guns that they had to push them out of the way to keep a clear field of fire.

The Japanese regiment that hit his sector was almost wiped out. Henderson Field held.

In May 1943 Basilone was awarded the Medal of Honor. He was sent home and became a national celebrity. Tens of thousands of people turned out for a parade in Raritan. He toured the country selling war bonds alongside Hollywood stars, and his picture was in Life magazine. The Marines offered him a commission and a safe job stateside for the rest of the war.

He turned them down. He said he wasn't an officer and wasn't a museum piece, and he belonged back with his men. They finally let him go back. He was assigned to train machine gunners for the new 5th Marine Division at Camp Pendleton in California.

There he met Lena Riggi, a sergeant in the Marine Corps Women's Reserve. They married in July 1944. A few months later he shipped out.

On Feb 19, 1945, he landed with the first waves on Iwo Jima. The beach was a nightmare of volcanic sand and Japanese artillery, and the Marines were pinned down. Basilone got his men moving. He helped knock out a Japanese blockhouse that was pouring fire onto the beach, then guided an American tank through a minefield under heavy fire. He pushed forward toward the edge of the island's first airfield.

That morning a mortar or artillery shell exploded near him and killed him. He was 28. He was awarded the Navy Cross. He's the only enlisted Marine in World War II to receive both the Medal of Honor and the Navy Cross.

Lena never remarried. When she died in 1999, she was buried wearing her wedding ring.

Two Navy destroyers have been named after him. There's a statue of him in Raritan, and the town still holds a parade in his honor. The road that runs through Camp Pendleton is called Basilone Road. Marines today still learn his name.

That shift is putting agentic AI at the centre of conversations about the future of technology—and it creates an important question: what infrastructure will these intelligent systems need to operate effectively?

TRON's participation in AGNTCon and MCPCon North America in San Jose, California, highlights its engagement with the rapidly evolving AI infrastructure community.

AI agents may eventually need to interact with digital assets, coordinate payments, access decentralised services, and execute transactions programmatically.

For these activities, blockchain infrastructure can offer useful capabilities:

🔹 Programmable transactions: Smart contracts can define transparent rules for how digital assets move and how certain actions are executed.

🔹 Verifiable activity: Public blockchain records allow transactions to be independently inspected, helping users audit what happened on-chain.

🔹 Digital asset infrastructure: Stablecoins and blockchain-based payments could provide mechanisms for transferring value between applications and services.

🔹 Open participation: Public blockchain networks can give developers access to shared infrastructure without requiring every application to build its own settlement layer.

These capabilities do not automatically make an AI agent secure or trustworthy. Identity, permissions, key management, privacy, and safeguards against unintended actions remain essential.

(If some of what follows is a repeat for you, I apologize. 
Aw, no I don't.)
I'm being asked about the new Netflix film, "Mosquito Bowl," about the Sixth Marine  Division's touch football game on Guadalcanal in late 1944, in advance of the horrific Battle of Okinawa. 
Why?
This is old territory for me.
Nearly 25 years ago, I researched the Mosquito Bowl as part of my Colorado  journalism work and my 2004 /2007 book "Third Down and a War to Go," about my father's 1942 Wisconsin Badgers. 
From starters to reserves, the Helms Foundation national champion Badgers made stunningly pervasive wartime contributions to the Allied cause in both Europe and the Pacific.  
Two top Badgers -- end Dave Schreiner, the '42 Big Ten MVP; and tackle Bob Baumann --  both served in the same Marine company, played in the Mosquito Bowl, and were killed in action on Okinawa. I made telling their stories a priority, though I encountered frustration along the way. That said, I ended up being given the family picture wallet that was with Dave Schreiner when he died.  
"Third Down and a War to Go" eventually drew rave reviews, most of which included a variation of: "This would make a great movie." I'm not going to give you faux modesty about that. Damn right, "Third Down and a War to Go," would have been a great movie. Yet neither the book's film rights nor my own screenplay version, which I completed in 2010, drew more than casual Hollywood interest as my agent and others sought offers. 
The opening pages of the "Third Down" screenplay:
https://t.co/ETVO7io6kk 
I failed. I was disappointed and a bit embittered.
At that point,  popular author Buzz Bissinger contacted me, saying he was starting work on a book about, yes, the Mosquito Bowl, focusing on the Marines who played in the game and died in action. That meant Schreiner and Baumann were integral elements of the storylines, but also that Buzz and I were coming at the tale from different angles.
Out of professional and personal respect, I granted Buzz access to  my Mosquito Bowl research. He didn't "rely" on it. Few of those I had interviewed were alive at the time by the time was doing his research. Ultimately, Buzz's 2022 book was excellent and included a stunning amount of deep-plot additional research. 
Here's my narrative of how that all went down. (This piece is where I'll be repeating myself, but please feel free to also wander on my site.) https://t.co/qDwa2ezNHu  
And here's my web site page on "Third Down and a War to Go":  https://t.co/g8k6wdTNEJ(That's the original hardback cover below.) 
Peter Berg and Mark Smith wrote the Mosquito Bowl screenplay.

text:
THREE YEARS AFTER FBI NOTIFIED MOTHER HER SON’S BODY WAS FOUND AT RETURN TO NATURE FUNERAL HOME, SHE IS STILL FIGHTING FOR ANSWERS

Denver mother Crystina Page reflects on the devastating discovery involving her son David, who was murdered in Monument, years of court battles, unanswered questions about his remains, and the creation of Colorado Remembers to support other families.

Saturday, October 24, 2026

DENVER, COLORADO — Three years after receiving a phone call that shattered what little peace she had found following her son’s murder, Denver resident Crystina Page is still searching for answers.

On the third anniversary of what she calls her “Notification Day,” Page shared a deeply personal account of the trauma, legal battles, and advocacy that have defined her life since learning that her son David’s body had been discovered at Return to Nature Funeral Home in Penrose, Colorado.

David was murdered in Monument. More than four years after his death, his body was discovered at the funeral home, despite his mother having believed for years that she had received his cremated remains.

“Three years ago today, a call from the FBI and coroner turned my world upside down,” Page wrote.

For four years, Page believed she had brought David home. She had mourned him, carried what she understood to be his ashes, and struggled to rebuild her life after losing her child.

Then came the call that changed everything.

“For four years, I thought I had brought David home. I had mourned him, carried his ashes, and tried to learn how to survive losing him. Then one phone call took even that small certainty away.”

A Mother Still Waiting for Answers

Three years after the discovery, Page says she still does not know whose remains she has.

She describes having cremated remains mixed with what she believed were her son’s, unidentified fingerprints, and hair whose origin remains unknown.

“I still don’t know whose cremated remains I have mixed with my son’s, or whose remains are in the jar with Grandma Fido. I don’t know whose fingerprints I have. I don’t know whose hair I have.”

The uncertainty has compounded the grief of losing her child.

Page says the discovery forced her to question everything she believed about her son’s final care, including whether the remains she had been given were actually his.

“All I know is that my son’s body was desecrated in the worst imaginable way,” she wrote.

The consequences have extended far beyond the courtroom.

Page describes continuing nightmares, a profound loss of trust in the funeral industry, and the emotional exhaustion of repeatedly reliving the circumstances surrounding her son’s death and the handling of his body.

“The nightmares don’t end because a hearing is over or a sentence has been handed down. I don’t believe they will ever go away.”

Years of Court Battles and a Historic Civil Judgment

The last three years have involved dozens of court appearances across federal, state, and civil proceedings.

Page and her family received what she describes as the largest civil judgment in Colorado history, although she does not expect to recover any of the money.

“We received the largest civil judgment in Colorado’s history, but we will never see a dime of it,” Page wrote.

Another civil case remains ahead, with a hearing expected in November.

For Page, the legal proceedings have meant repeatedly confronting disturbing details about what happened inside Return to Nature Funeral Home.

She also describes learning about aquamation experiments and continuing to question what information has yet to be disclosed.

The experience has shaken her trust in an industry families depend on during some of the most vulnerable moments of their lives.

“How do you trust someone to care for another being you love after learning what happened to the child you entrusted to someone else?”

Page credits Bianca, Be a Tree Cremation, and Water Bridge Aquamation with helping restore some of her faith in an industry that had otherwise betrayed her trust.

Turning Grief Into Advocacy: Colorado Remembers

Despite the ongoing trauma, Page has transformed much of her grief into advocacy for other families.

She helped establish Colorado Remembers, a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting families, preserving the memory of loved ones, and advocating for accountability and changes in the funeral industry.

The organization has brought families together through candlelight vigils, memorial events, fundraisers, and community gatherings.

Its work includes a wind phone installation at Concrete Couch, offering people a place to sit, pick up a telephone, and symbolically speak to someone they have lost.

For Page, these spaces provide something court proceedings cannot: connection with people who understand the experience of loss.

“Behind each one are people carrying their own grief who still show up for one another,” she wrote.

“Those moments matter to me—the hugs, the names spoken out loud, the chance to be with people who understand without needing an explanation.”

Colorado Remembers has become a source of support for families who have experienced unimaginable losses, many of whom have found themselves navigating complicated legal proceedings, unanswered questions, and profound distrust of the systems responsible for caring for their loved ones.

What began in grief has grown into an effort to make sure those families are not forgotten.

Pushing for Legislative Change and Stronger Oversight

Page’s advocacy has also extended into Colorado’s regulatory and legislative systems.

She has worked with the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies and testified before both the Colorado House and Senate in support of legislation and stronger oversight.

Her objective is to prevent other families from experiencing what hers has endured.

“That work takes time and energy I sometimes don’t know how to find. But I know what it costs when the protections aren’t there.”

The organization has also reached a significant milestone.

Colorado Remembers has received approval to move forward with two locations: an educational center in Calhan and the MontemAra Memorial Preserve.

The Calhan facility is envisioned as a place for education, advocacy, storytelling, and legislative work.

MontemAra Memorial Preserve is intended to give families a dedicated place to remember and honor their loved ones.

“I want families to have somewhere they can go and know their person matters,” Page wrote.

The projects represent an important step in the organization’s mission to turn the experiences of affected families into lasting education, remembrance, and reform.

The Personal Toll Behind the Public Advocacy

While Page has become an outspoken advocate, the public sees only part of what families endure.

Her experiences have included extensive media interviews, sharing her family’s story through Curious Case of the Funeral Home of Horrors and Talk Gruesome To Me, and repeatedly describing traumatic events she would rather never have experienced.

She has also navigated the death of her mother while continuing to cope with the aftermath of the funeral home discovery.

Page credits friends, fellow advocates, and family members with helping her survive the past three years.

She offered particular gratitude to her sister, Tonia, who answered the phone when Page first learned what had happened.

“You answered the only phone call that has ever mattered,” she wrote.

“I thought my soul was ripping apart, and didn’t question who would answer.”

She says that support helped her endure the first moments after the notification and the difficult years that followed.

Along the way, Page has formed friendships with people she might never have met under different circumstances.

They have shared grief, anger, legal struggles, and moments of laughter.

“I wish we had met under different circumstances. I am so grateful we found each other.”

She also acknowledged those who have supported her through moments of anger, exhaustion, and overwhelming grief.

“Through all of this, people have stood beside me when I have been angry, exhausted, overwhelmed, and hard to reach. To those who have stayed, listened, shown up, and loved me through it: thank you.”

Three Years Later, the Fight Continues

The Return to Nature Funeral Home case has left families confronting questions that extend far beyond criminal sentences and civil judgments.

For Crystina Page, the central issue remains deeply personal: what happened to her son David, what happened to his remains, and why so many questions remain unanswered.

Even as Colorado Remembers expands its efforts to support other families and pursue meaningful changes in Colorado law, Page continues to live with the uncertainty surrounding her son.

Her anniversary message is a reminder that behind every court proceeding, investigation, and headline is a family whose life has been permanently altered.

No financial judgment can return her son. No criminal sentence can erase the years she spent believing she had brought him home when his body remained inside a funeral home.

And no legal victory can undo the trauma of discovering that the remains a family trusted someone to care for were not handled as promised.

“Three years later, I am still David’s mom. I still miss him every day. I am still angry. I still need answers.”

Despite everything she has endured, Page has made clear that she has no intention of giving up.

“And I am still here, fighting for my son and for every family who deserves to know what happened to someone they love.”

Denver in the Dark

Disclosure: The publisher of Denver in the Dark serves on the Board of Directors of Colorado Remembers and has been personally involved in supporting Crystina Page and other affected families.

text:
Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears

Oct 23 (Reuters) - With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.

His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, eased sanctions on Russian ​fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. 

Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to ‌the polls.Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters.

 Nearly 80% of Americans blame Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll.

US diesel prices rose nearly 10 cents a gallon in the latest week to an average of $6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration.Diesel in the last two months has become a central issue not only in the midterms but as a catalyst driving up already-elevated US inflation. 

The fuel is critical for farmers, construction companies, freight operators ​and more, and government data last week showed its rise was partly behind hefty increases in delivery costs, early-stage food production costs and even toy prices.

The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like Iowa ​and Kansas, where rising fuel and fertilizer costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump's core supporters.

Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign rallies across ⁠the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced $8 billion in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Monday.

The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in ​pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. 

Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel ​exports, has created diplomatic friction.

" The president tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here,”

 said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania.

The White House attributed high diesel prices to

 “pre-existing issues,”

 including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia's war in Ukraine, while defending Trump's efforts to ease costs.

text:
Lightning burned Tuskegee Institute's chapel to the ground in January 1957, and five months later the Alabama legislature redrew the town so that the school was no longer inside it. The Supreme Court later described what the new twenty-eight-sided city limit did: it removed all but four or five of Tuskegee's four hundred Black voters, and not one white voter or resident. The school's alumni raised the money and rebuilt the chapel anyway, and two Black architects who had each run its architecture department drew the set it was built from.

In 1923, Tuskegee Institute handed a young man a certificate. It said plumbing.

His name was John A. Welch. He had arrived on that campus in 1920, and the paper in his hand said that he could fit pipe.

That was not a small thing at Tuskegee, and it was never meant as one.

Booker T. Washington had staked the whole school on the argument that a man who could do skilled work with his hands could not be talked out of his own worth. So the place turned out bricklayers, carpenters, wheelwrights and plumbers, deliberately.

For almost four decades after the school opened, the building course included time in the campus brickworks. Students dug local clay, pressed it into moulds, fired it, and laid it into the walls of their own school.

They sold what was left over to bring money in. The campus was, in a real sense, made out of the students who lived on it.

And every one of them worshipped in the same room.

Attendance was required, at daily vespers and again on Sunday. Whatever else a Tuskegee student did in a week, he sat in that building.

The room was the chapel Robert R. Taylor designed and students built between 1896 and 1898.

It took 1,200,000 of those handmade bricks. When it was finished it was the first building in Macon County to have electric lights, wired by the school's own electrical division.

It seated about twenty-four hundred people, which was most of the school at once.

That is the room John Welch sat in while he was learning to sweat a joint.

He did not stay a plumber. He went to Howard University and took his architecture degree in 1930, studying under Albert Cassell, who was at that moment designing most of the Howard campus himself.

Welch stayed on at Howard five more years. Then he went into the drafting rooms of Hilyard Robinson, Ervin Porter and Paul Revere Williams, three of the most accomplished Black architects working in America, and he drew for them.

In 1940 Tuskegee called him home, and not to fit pipe.

They made him director of the Department of Architecture and Mechanical Drawing, the department Robert R. Taylor had built. The chair had just been vacated by a man named Louis Edwin Fry Sr., who had held it since 1935.

Fry came out of Bastrop, Texas, and a segregated school called Emile High, where he finished the twelfth grade at fifteen years old.

He took a science degree at Prairie View in 1922, then Kansas State, for a bachelor's in architectural engineering in 1927 and a master's in 1929. He went to work under Albert Cassell at Howard too, on the Founders Library, on Douglas Hall, on the gate you walk through to get onto that campus.

Tuskegee offered him the department in 1935 and he took it. Five years later he handed it to Welch and went to Lincoln University in Missouri as campus architect.

Welch went into the Army.

Fry went back to school. In 1945, at forty-two years old, with his son enrolled at a high school in Roxbury, he took a master of architecture from the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

He worked a short while for Marcel Breuer, went back to Lincoln, then to Howard University in 1947, where he stayed twenty-five years. He got the architecture departments at both Tuskegee and Howard through to accreditation, which is what puts a graduate on the road to a licence.

Welch came out of the Army and went to Washington too. In 1954 the two of them put both their names on one door.

Fry and Welch built at Black colleges. Sixteen buildings across five states, and eventually something close to a third of the Tuskegee campus.

The states a man can build in are the states that will license him. Fry held a licence in Alabama, Missouri, Maryland, Pennsylvania and the District of Columbia.

Alabama mattered most of the five. By the middle of the 1950s Fry and Welch were the firm Tuskegee called, and they gave the school its new engineering building, Moton Hall, in 1956.

Then came the night of 23 January 1957.

Lightning struck Taylor's chapel. It did not survive the night.

The room those students had raised, the wiring they had run and the windows all came down together.

The windows had gone in during a renovation in 1932, designed by the artist Katherine Lamb Tait, eleven of them carrying eleven Negro spirituals in glass. At the dedication in April 1933 the choir had stood underneath them and sung all eleven straight through.

Welch had sat in that room as a trade student, and Fry had run the architecture department on that same campus. Between them they were going to have to replace it.

Less than five months later the State of Alabama did something worse to that campus than the lightning had.

On 13 June 1957 both houses of the Alabama legislature passed Senate Bill 291 without a single vote against it. It became Local Act 140 without the governor's signature on it.

It was written by state senator Sam Engelhardt, who was also executive secretary of the White Citizens' Council of Alabama. It redrew the city limits of Tuskegee.

The town had been a square. Act 140 turned it into a twenty-eight-sided figure.

The new line put Tuskegee Institute outside the city altogether. When the Supreme Court came to describe the effect of it, the Court put it this way: the act removed all but four or five of the city's four hundred Black voters, and not one white voter or resident.

The school that had given John Welch his certificate was now outside the town it was named for.

Engelhardt did not hide the reason. He said in plain terms that people like him could not stand the prospect of a Black man sitting in the Alabama legislature.

On 25 June 1957, three thousand people came to Butler Chapel African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church in town, which is the church whose grounds held the shanty where Tuskegee opened in 1881. Only about five hundred could fit inside, and the rest stood outside and listened.

Charles Gomillion, a sociology professor and the dean of students at the Institute, asked them to stop spending money at white-owned businesses in Tuskegee. They called it trading with friends.

They held to it for three and a half years, and stores in that town went under.

On 4 August 1957, six weeks after that meeting, Gomillion and twelve others sued the mayor. Two federal courts threw the case out before the Supreme Court reversed them on 14 November 1960 and sent it back down to Alabama.

On 17 February 1961 a district judge named Frank M. Johnson Jr. struck Act 140 down for good. The square came back, and the boycott ended that same month.

That was the ground the new chapel was raised on. A school that had just lost the building it worshipped in, in a town that had just voted to pretend the school was not there.

They rebuilt anyway.

President Luther H. Foster and his trustees started planning almost at once, and alumni across the country sent in the money.

The chapel was going to be handled differently from Moton Hall. The school wanted the biggest name in American architecture on it.

Paul Rudolph's office was already drawing a new master plan for the campus, and in 1960 he took the chapel commission.

What Rudolph published that year was concrete. Sculptural, sharply angled, poured in place, the kind of building making his name at the time.

Then the estimates came back and the arithmetic did not work. Concrete was going to cost more than Tuskegee had.

So in 1965 the drawings went to Fry and Welch, and they began the work of getting the building actually built in another material.

Welch was doing this while running a college. He was Dean of the School of Applied Sciences at Tuskegee through those years, and Fry was chairing a department at Howard, up in Washington.

They redrew it as a steel frame wearing a skin of brick.

Nobody demanded brick out of reverence for the campus, which is what the sentimental version of this story says. Money forced the question.

What happened next is that two men who knew that campus down to its clay were the ones who answered it.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating

Rudolph wanted brick that would read as one continuous mass rather than as stacked courses, the way poured concrete reads, and he backed the change instead of fighting it.

Rudolph had come up much the way they had. Born in Kentucky and raised in Alabama, schooled in the South, he took his graduate degree at the Harvard Graduate School of Design under Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer.

Fry had taken his Harvard degree in the same school under the same two men. Welch, like Rudolph, had served in the United States military.

So Fry and Welch specified a pinkish mortar cut to the colour of the brick, so that thousands of separate units would look to the eye like a single surface. They drew angled piers and overlapping corners that no mason could build from a standard detail.

The brick itself had to come from somewhere else. By 1967 the Tuskegee brickworks was gone, and the school that had made 1,200,000 bricks for its own chapel had to buy the brick for the new one.

Somebody had to stand on the site while that brick went up. Major L. Holland took his degree at Howard in 1964, worked for Fry in Washington and for Rudolph in New York, and in 1968 came home to Tuskegee as the project representative from Fry and Welch's office.

He never left, and taught architecture on that campus until 2004.

Construction on the chapel ran from 1967 to 1969. It came in at two million dollars, twice the original budget, and the rest of the campus master plan around it was never built at all.

What opened in 1969 has no right angles in it anywhere.

The sanctuary runs roughly eighty feet by a hundred and seventy, and the ceiling climbs and falls as you move down it. Daylight comes in sideways, through a continuous slot of glass running the whole perimeter just under the roof.

The roof itself is a warped surface carried on closely spaced steel joists, shaped that way for sound, because the building had to work as a concert hall for the Tuskegee choir.

It seats twelve hundred. That is half of what Taylor's chapel held.

In the entrance hall they set reproductions of the Singing Windows, rebuilt from Katherine Lamb Tait's surviving designs, because the glass itself was ash. They also set a single brick into that wall, taken from the house Booker T. Washington had lived in.

The chapel stands between the campus cemetery, where Washington and George Washington Carver are buried, and the monument raised to Washington in 1922.

James Earl Massey, who served as dean of that chapel, said the interior reminds a person of "the roughness of life," because the bricks are irregular on purpose and keep calling attention to themselves.

The construction drawings that told a contractor how to build any of that were developed in the office of Fry and Welch, working with Rudolph.

The reviews were enormous. Architectural Record ran the building as its November 1969 cover story, and its editor called the interior one of the most dramatic and powerful religious spaces built in the century.

The cover line read: A Chapel for Tuskegee by Rudolph.

Neither Fry nor Welch is in the title.

In 1968, the year before it opened and with the walls in Alabama partly raised, the American Institute of Architects invited Whitney M. Young Jr. of the National Urban League to give the keynote at its national convention in Portland. He told a room full of American architects that on civil rights they were most distinguished by their "thunderous silence and complete irrelevance."

There were somewhere around fifty-six thousand practising architects in America at the turn of that decade. The Black ones were scarce enough that the Black men sitting in that Portland room had mostly never met each other.

Three years later, at the AIA convention in Detroit in 1971, twelve of them decided to do something about it.

Louis Fry Sr. was one of them. He was sixty-eight years old and two years past the opening of the finest building his office ever put its seal on.

One of the first things they sat down to work out was how to lobby Washington so that Black architects would be written into federal building legislation at all. They met again on 12 November 1971 in Nassau and adopted a constitution.

That is the National Organization of Minority Architects, and it still exists.

Fry and Welch itself had closed in 1969. Both partners retired and Fry's son took the practice over.

John A. Welch was made a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 1987. Louis Fry Sr. died in Washington on 10 June 2000, at ninety-seven years old, having taught architecture to hundreds of Black students who would not have been taught it anywhere else.

The chapel became a destination. Architecture students still drive into Macon County to stand inside it.

In 2025 the Yale Architecture Gallery finally laid the two drawing sets on two tables, Rudolph's 1960 concrete scheme on one and Fry and Welch's construction set on the other, and let visitors turn the pages. They were facsimiles, because the originals sit in the Library of Congress and the gallery is not built to hold them, and the show travelled on to Tuskegee, to MIT, and to the National Building Museum.

The credit was never hidden. It had been printed on those drawings the entire time, in the words the profession uses for it.

Architects of record. It means the people legally answerable for the thing standing up, the ones whose seal goes on the sheets, the ones the law comes to if it falls.

To everybody else, it looks like filing.
