text:
They sold the plows, the mules and a man on the same December afternoon in 1848. Jefferson Belton was singled out in the will to be sold instead of freed, and his family stood on the ground they were about to sail from and watched him go under the hammer.

His children had no money to buy their own father and had already written begging the executors to just let him go. A stranger bought him at that sale and set him free so he could follow them, and the executor never lifted a finger.

A man sat down with an envelope, turned it over, and wrote on the back of it that he had not been anywhere near the killings.

He was careful about the number. Four, he put down, and he had nothing to do with it, was not in the neighborhood at the time, and certainly disapproved.

He called it the destruction of some of the negroes. Destruction is the word a man uses about property.

His name was Isaac Ross Wade, and the four men were Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary and Esau.

Nobody in Jefferson County, Mississippi wrote those names down anywhere else. They exist because the man who was supposed to have set them free scribbled a denial on scrap paper and somebody kept it.

Start with the house, because they built it. Prospect Hill stood on a rise six miles outside Lorman, with four thousand eight hundred and eighty acres of cotton falling away from it.

A descendant writing in 1947 described a two-story building put up entirely from lumber made on the place, sawed by the people held there. They dressed the poplar ceiling boards by hand and wainscoted the hall, the dining room and the parlor in cherry.

A bookcase of choice cherry ran to the ceiling. The staircase came up from the front of the hall on cherry handrails, and every plank of it was cut from trees on ground they did not own.

Captain Isaac Ross had come out of the Revolution with a glass eye in place of the one he lost in the fighting. He built the place into an empire, helped found the Mississippi Colonization Society, and in 1834 wrote a will that stunned his family.

The will did not take effect at his death. It waited on his daughter Margaret Reed, and she died in 1838.

So from 1838, every adult at Prospect Hill knew a piece of paper existed with their names on it and the word freedom attached.

They also knew the executor. Isaac Ross Wade was the old man's grandson, raised under his wing from the age of six.

He moved into the mansion house and went to court. His argument was that the dead man had no right to give away what he considered his.

For ten years those people worked cotton for a man actively suing to keep them. Under the will they were already technically free and owed wages, and Wade paid nothing.

They did not sit still for it. Men hauled bales by ox and mule down to the river landing at Rodney, and on those trips, sometimes without passes, they slipped off to meet colonization agents and old friends of Captain Ross who could tell them where the case stood.

None of them had standing in any Mississippi courtroom. They were leaving a plantation without permission to get a status report on a lawsuit about their own bodies.

In 1841 the Wades went to the legislature to have the will voided by statute. A lawmaker told Dr. John Ker, the society's agent, that if the legislature would not kill the wills then two hundred armed men in Jefferson County were ready to.

That bill failed. In 1842 a revised one passed, written to strip the force from any Mississippi will that freed people on condition they leave the state.

Cotton was planted and cotton was picked, and the ocean stayed five thousand miles away. By the spring of 1845 a group of them had stopped waiting on the courts.

On the evening of 14 April the house was full. Wade, his wife, three small children, his sister Adelaide Richardson and her three, his brother Dr. Walter Wade, a business partner, and a young houseguest named Mary Girault.

The cook put something in the after-supper coffee. Most of the adults drank it, and Dr. Wade and Miss Girault did not.

Somewhere past midnight, with the drug taking hold, somebody set the pitch pine alight.

Everything anybody knows about the next hour comes from the family who was inside it, printed in a Port Gibson paper fifty-seven years later by Wade's son. Read it knowing whose account it is.

Dr. Wade woke first and could not rouse the household. By his nephew's telling he would probably have failed, in a house that size, without the help of a man named Major, Wade's own bodyservant, who went through the rooms with him.

Major had every reason on earth to let that house burn. He went room to room with Dr. Wade until the household was on its feet.

Downstairs, Wade wrestled the front door open and stood back from it. Miss Girault had already come out another way with the two youngest Richardson children, having asked Adelaide to bring down the eldest.

They counted heads in the yard and Martha was not there. She was five years old and still upstairs in bed, and her mother had walked out without her.

Adelaide Richardson turned and screamed for somebody to go back in with her.

A man named Thomas answered. He went up the cherry staircase beside her, the one their own people had built by hand.

The steps sank under them into the fire.

Both of them were dragged back out badly burned. Adelaide had to be pulled clear by her hair.

They found the child's heart in the ashes the next morning and buried it in the family graveyard, a few paces from where she died.

One thing in that yard has never sat still. When Wade forced the front door open, a man was standing outside it in the dark holding an axe.

His name was Esau. Mary Girault came through that doorway before Wade did, unexpectedly, and saw him there with the blade up.

She spoke first. She asked him, calling him uncle, whether he had come to help them by cutting the door away.

He said yes ma'am, and he walked off.

The family concluded afterward that Esau had waited at that door a long while and made no move to wake anyone or break it in. He was there, they decided, to kill Wade the moment he came through it.

That may be exactly right. What the record holds is a white girl handing him a way out of the moment, Esau taking it, and a man walking out of that house alive after ten years in court to keep him in the field.

The reckoning came without a courthouse.

A posse went through the quarters on the strength of rumor. Men were taken out and hanged on the white oaks at Prospect Hill, in sight of the smoking foundation of the house they had built, within a stone's throw of the grave of the man who had signed their freedom eleven years before.

How many is not a settled question. Wade's own note says four, his son's account says Esau and six or seven others were burnt or hanged, and other tellings put the figure at ten, eleven, a dozen.

No trial was held. No inquest, no charge against anybody, and the overseer stayed on the place two more years before collecting his final wages at the end of 1847.

The only figure written down at the time sits on the back of that envelope. A man put it there to establish he was elsewhere.

Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary and Esau are the four he named. Everyone else who died that spring is a number somebody guessed at later.

On 16 December 1847, thirty-four of them were gathered into a room to vote.

It was a cold morning. Ker stood in front of them and talked about Captain Ross, the will, the ten years of court, while several white men waited along the wall to witness what came next.

Then he asked the adults the only question the paper allowed him to ask.

Did they elect to go to Liberia, where they would be freed, or remain in Mississippi to be sold.

Every adult in that room said go.

Ker went down the sheet writing the same three words beside every name. Elected to go, elected to go, elected to go, and a line at the bottom recording that they each and all made their election.

Not every name got an answer beside it. Beside the children he wrote under age, and beside Lucy Ross, a grown woman past twenty-one, he recorded that she was not competent to vote because of her disability.

The ballot offered an ocean crossing or the auction block at home. Of 4,571 people who had reached Liberia between 1820 and 1843, only 1,819 were still alive there in 1843.

Thirty-four of them chose the ocean.

They rode down to Rodney on 28 December and boarded the steamboat Natchez. In New Orleans they waited in boarding houses while a hired carpenter built bunks into a ship.

The barque Nehemiah Rich sailed on 7 January 1848. Ten weeks later it put them ashore at Greenville, on the Sinoe River.

A woman named Sarah J. Woodson wrote back to Mississippi that May. She described the gale that hit them on the thirtieth of January and said she had thought they would never see land again.

Then she mentioned the thing she could not stop turning over. She had left her feather bed at Prospect Hill and had no way of getting another one.

She had crossed an ocean out of slavery, and what she wanted her old mistress to know was that she had nothing to sleep on.

The rest stayed behind for one more crop. The society had spent its money on lawyers, so a hundred and forty people worked another full year of cotton to pay for their own passage.

Then the horses and mules took sick with glanders and died, and Ker had to buy livestock before the fields could be worked at all.

On 22 December 1848 an auction was held at Prospect Hill. They sold the farm equipment, and they sold one man.

Jefferson Belton had been singled out in the will to be sold rather than freed. His family stood on the same ground they were about to sail from and watched him go under the hammer with the plows.

His children had already written pleading for him. They had no money to buy their own father, so they asked the executors to simply let him go, and nobody did.

The man who bought him at that sale turned around and freed him, so he could follow his family across the ocean. A stranger at an auction did what the executor would not.

A year later the barque Laura carried the rest of them out of New Orleans, on 22 January 1849. The passenger list holds a hundred and forty-one people freed by Captain Ross, and one more freed by his daughter.

How many of them saw Liberia is a question the record does not answer cleanly. The state archives in Jackson, drawing on a Wade family history written in 1947, say only ninety reached their destination.

If that figure is right, fifty-one people who were freed in Mississippi died getting to the place they were freed to go. Nobody wrote down their names either.

The ones who landed arrived owning nothing.

Nobody ever sold the 4,880 acres for them, and the estate they had been told was worth a hundred thousand dollars never reached them. Wade settled with the society in 1850 by keeping the land and dropping his claim to the money.

He put up a new house on that ground in 1854. It is still standing.

Seventy-five years later Mississippi decided to do the whole thing again, at scale, without asking anybody.

On 20 February 1922 the state Senate passed Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 21, twenty-five votes to nine. Senator Torrey George McCallum of Laurel had written it, asking President Harding to trade off part of Europe's war debt for territory in Africa and settle every Black resident of the state there permanently.

The document called it a final home. The 1920 census had counted 935,184 Black Mississippians against 853,962 white ones.

A majority of the state was being voted out of the country by a chamber almost none of them had helped elect. The 1890 constitution had seen to that.

The House killed it on 10 March, forty to thirty-two. Not one word of the surviving debate turns on anybody's conscience.

Representative John Holmes Sherard objected that it would cost the Delta its labor. He told the chamber he had five hundred Black people on his plantation in Coahoma County and had never had a quarrel with a one of them.

They were kept because the crop had to come in.

Nobody in that building seems to have checked the census. Mississippi counted 1,009,487 Black residents in 1910 and 935,184 in 1920, a drop of seventy-four thousand in a decade when births still outran deaths.

That means the true number who left was higher than the fall in the count, and the Great Migration was already carrying them. No treaty, no war debt, no ship and no senator was required.

Back at Prospect Hill, Granville Woodson had been sixteen on the morning of the vote and got marked under age. In Greenville he went to school for the first time in his life.

His father Pascal could not read or write, so for years afterward it was Granville who wrote the family's letters back to Mississippi. The boy the record would not let answer a question became the one doing the writing.

Isaac Ross Wade died on 10 January 1891, at seventy-six. They buried him in the Prospect Hill cemetery with his people, and set his headstone facing the opposite direction from every other marker in that ground.

Nobody has ever explained it. It could be an oversight, and it could be that somebody who knew what happened on those oaks decided where he would be looking.

Captain Isaac Ross lies a few yards away under marble shipped from Philadelphia down to Natchez and on to Rodney, with three inscriptions cut into it praising his support of colonization. Photographed in 2023, that stone has weathered to the edge of unreadable.

In a separate burying ground on the same property there is no granite and no marble at all, not for any of the people who cut the cherry, sawed the planks, carried the cotton and died there.

Twenty-three acres are held now by the Archaeological Conservancy, kept standing on donations. The digs there are trying to work out where these people slept and cooked, and what they carried onto the ships.

No shovel is going to turn up Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary or Esau.

Their only record is a denial written on the back of an envelope. We have their names because a man wanted it known he was not there.

Take them off his envelope. Andrew, Gilbert, Yeary, Esau.

text:
$WLFI : What If World Liberty Financial Became More Than a Crypto Project?

1. What if WLFI did not merely outperform XRP, but evolved into an Ethereum-scale ecosystem with the institutional influence of JPMorgan?

2. That would require more than a token rally; it would require an entirely new financial architecture.

3. At its center would be USD1, a dollar-backed stablecoin connecting institutional capital, global payments, digital assets, and on-chain financial markets.

4. The real opportunity would not be USD1's market capitalization alone, but its potential to become a settlement asset used across exchanges, institutions, and decentralized finance.

5. Every new use case could reinforce the next: deeper liquidity attracts users, users attract developers and institutions, and a larger ecosystem generates more financial activity.

6. This is where Ethereum becomes the relevant comparison: independent applications creating demand for one another rather than relying on speculation alone.

7. But ecosystem growth is only half the equation.

8. If USD1 became a major financial instrument while WLFI remained a governance token without economic rights, the businesses behind the ecosystem could capture the value while token holders captured very little.

9. This is the fundamental distinction between protocol adoption and token value accrual.

10. JPMorgan offers a different model: diversified financial services, durable customer relationships, sustainable earnings, and a corporate structure connecting business performance to shareholder value.

11. For WLFI to approach this model, its surrounding businesses would need to generate sustainable revenue from payments, institutional infrastructure, tokenization, and financial services.

12. More importantly, that economic success must connect directly to WLFI.

13. Potential mechanisms include transparent buybacks, supply reduction, formally established economic rights, or indispensable token utility, none of which should be assumed without verification.

14. The strongest scenario combines three engines: XRP-like institutional connectivity, Ethereum-like network effects, and JPMorgan-like earning power.

15. These engines reinforce one another only when real activity generates sustainable earnings and WLFI captures a measurable share of the value.

16. That connection determines whether WLFI benefits from the ecosystem or merely shares its name.

17. If this architecture scaled globally, USD1 could become a widely used settlement instrument while WLFI gained an economic foundation beyond speculation.

18. The market could then value WLFI according to its utility, scarcity, strategic importance, and value-capture mechanisms rather than political branding alone.

19. Yet a trillion-dollar token is not equivalent to a trillion-dollar financial institution; market capitalization is not corporate revenue, assets, or shareholder equity.

20. The strongest bullish thesis is not that USD1 growth automatically makes WLFI valuable.

21. It is that USD1 could anchor a global financial network while WLFI becomes an asset whose holders have a demonstrable economic stake in its success.

22. If institutional adoption, ecosystem expansion, profitability, and token value capture converge, WLFI could occupy a fundamentally different position in digital finance.

23. The ultimate question is not how large World Liberty Financial could become.

24. It is whether WLFI holders will own a meaningful share of the upside when it does.

text:
Timepass talk on Sunday

1. Caliber Mining and Logistics

Caliber Mining and Logistics is an integrated mining services company providing end-to-end solutions across the coal mining value chain. The company undertakes overburden (OB) removal, coal extraction, coal logistics, rake loading, rail coordination services, and coal trading.

Caliber Mining’s Q1 looked ugly on the surface: EBITDA margin dropped to 17% from its usual 24-28% range. But the cause was external and specific. The Iran war situation sent bulk/commercial diesel from about ₹90 a litre to a peak of ₹154, and while most of Caliber’s coal mining contracts carry fuel escalation clauses, those clauses lag and don’t pass through 100% of the increase. So the company absorbed a chunk of the spike in a single quarter. Management called it temporary and guided to a normalized margin of around 23% once fuel costs settle.

What makes this worth discussing now is Coal India’s new diesel compensation mechanism. It replaces the interim arrangements with a method that compensates 100% of diesel price increases, based on bulk rates and standard consumption norms rather than retail pump prices and fixed formulas. It is effective from March 20, 2026, and applies retrospectively to contracts with subsidiaries like WCL and NCL, with amounts already received under the interim arrangements to be reconciled. In effect, the exact gap that caused the Q1 miss, partial and delayed pass-through, is being closed after the fact.

The bull case is that Q1 is the trough, margins head back toward 23%, and a retrospective true-up could even give a one-time lift in coming quarters. The things to check are the direction and size of the reconciliation (it could be a receivable or a clawback), whether bulk-rate compensation fully matches what Caliber actually pays for diesel, how much of the order book sits outside WCL and NCL, and whether the cash actually arrives, since working capital could lag the margin recovery.

2. Cohance Lifesciences

Who is Cohance: Cohance Lifesciences is an Indian technology-led, integrated CDMO majority-owned by Advent International, formed when Suven Pharmaceuticals merged with Advent’s privately held Cohance Lifesciences effective May 1, 2025. It runs three businesses: Pharma CDMO (39% of FY26 sales, including ADCs, oligonucleotides and the Sapala and NJ Bio subsidiaries), API+ (48%) and Specialty Chemicals (13%). Mix has shifted sharply in the latest quarter: API+ was 62% of Q1 FY27 revenue, Pharma CDMO 30% and Specialty Chemicals 8%. Leadership has been turbulent: MD Dr. V. Prasada Raju resigned in October 2025, Executive Chairman Vivek Sharma stepped down in April 2026, and Umang Vohra, formerly of Cipla, took over as Executive Chairman and Group CEO in May 2026 on a term through April 2031. The company is also moving to consolidate its nucleic-acid business by raising its stake in Sapala, which it bought 67.5% of in July 2024 for ₹258 crore.

What went wrong: FY26 was a transition year, with revenue down about 13% and EBITDA margin falling from roughly 31% to 19%. The causes were destocking in two high-margin commercial molecules (about ₹260 crore), customer-led delays on Phase 2/3 programmes, the US FDA action at Nacharam, the biotech funding winter at NJ Bio, and API+ softness. Q1 FY27 was worse and was labelled a “bottoming out” quarter. Revenue fell 23.1% to ₹4,223 Mn, adjusted EBITDA margin collapsed to 2.2% from 24.4%, and the company posted an adjusted loss of ₹430 Mn. Management blames shipment phasing in Pharma CDMO, an H2-weighted AgChem schedule, lower formulations revenue, an unfavourable mix and negative operating leverage. Standalone adjusted EBITDA margin was 9.2%, so the gap to the consolidated 2.2% comes from the subsidiaries, with NJ Bio alone losing ₹328 Mn at EBITDA. ROCE has fallen to 6.3% from 26.9% in FY25. Two cautions are my own inferences, not the deck’s. Pharma CDMO’s 38.7% drop includes Sapala’s 2.5x growth, so the small-molecule decline underneath is steeper. And the ₹1,063 Mn free cash flow came mostly from receivables falling about ₹1,950 Mn, not from earnings.

What the future holds: Management’s guidance is that Q2 will be better than Q1, H2 will be better YoY, and EBITDA recovery will be H2-weighted, with FY27 still framed as a growth year. The supports are two molecules in commercial supply with deliveries in Q2 and Q3, a restocking order for the destocked product, two more launches in 12–15 months, a 10-molecule Phase III pipeline with 140+ active projects, and Sapala’s confirmed order book and new amidites capacity. API+ is expected to be stable in H1, and Nacharam US supplies have restarted. AgChem is a longer wait: FY27 is mainly customer qualification, with a key programme becoming meaningful from FY28. The risks are NJ Bio (FTE-contract risk, with revenue visibility only as the new facility opens), the pace of Nacharam’s remediation, and the cost of the Sapala buyout and amidites ramp against a thin earnings base. 

3. Supreme Court Rap, 30% Cap, and the Oncology Selloff: What Beta Drugs and Sakar Healthcare Say

The backdrop: Trade margin rationalization is not a new discussion. It has been on the government’s radar for years, with an earlier intervention on selected anti-cancer drugs in 2019 itself. But the Supreme Court’s sharp remarks in September turned a long-running policy debate into an immediate flashpoint for the pharma industry.

The episode began with a PIL by Kishan Chand Jain before Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta. On September 22, the court called the pricing of a cancer drug with a ₹2,700 retailer price and a ₹27,000 MRP “broad daylight dacoity”. On September 29, it called 10-fold hospital markups “carnage” and suggested a uniform 16% margin on all medicines. On October 12, the Centre told the court it would cap trade margins on anti-cancer drugs at 30% of MRP. The bench asked why the cap covered only cancer drugs. The NPPA then notified the cap on 137 drugs on October 17, effective November 9. The next hearing is October 27.

What the companies said: Sakar’s October 14 NSE filing says its business is skewed towards oncology exports, so the domestic cap doesn’t affect it. It cites the ET report that the move regulates only trade margins, not manufacturers’ prices or revenues. On its October 22 call, Beta called the impact “zero or negligible”. Of ₹123 crore in FY26 branded sales, about ₹60 crore is orals sold through distributors, and about ₹50 crore of the ₹63 crore in injectables is scheduled drugs with government-fixed MRPs. The remaining ₹13 crore of non-scheduled injectables, it said, sees no margin or realisation impact.

The callout: The logic holds because the cap targets hospital, retailer and distributor markups, not the manufacturer’s price. Beta looks safest on orals and less certain on hospital-channel injectables, where it gave few details. Sakar is protected mainly by its export focus.

The October 27 hearing is the key risk to watch. Any broader margin regulation would weaken the “oncology-only” argument that hospitals and pharma companies have been relying on. If the directive is extended to all critical drugs, the impact could be much wider and deeper!

4. Centum Electronics (Blast from the past)

Centum Electronics designs and makes the specialized electronic brains (ESDM) and control systems that run fighter jets, space satellites, and missiles. They sell these high-precision circuit boards and sensors to major aerospace companies and government space agencies who need to make sure their equipment works perfectly in extreme conditions where failure is not an option. These electronic systems sit at the core of critical applications like advanced radar systems, military communication networks, and onboard controllers for space payloads.

How they make money?

A. Build-to-Specification (BTS): ~28% of Revenue

BTS designs and manufactures custom electronic systems for defence, aerospace, and space, including radar, electronic warfare and space payloads. Recent wins include the ₹570 crore lifecycle AESA radar program for HAL’s UHM platform and a ₹30+ crore space debris tracking radar.

It is a higher-margin business (~20% EBITDA), but has longer execution cycles of around 2–2.5 years, making it a strategically important, albeit smaller, part of the business.

B. Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS): ~72% of Revenue

EMS provides contract manufacturing across industrial electronics, electrification, grid automation, semiconductor equipment and defence. A key anchor customer is a leading semiconductor equipment OEM, where Centum is ramping up production.

EMS is a lower-margin business (~9–11% EBITDA) but offers more recurring, annuity-like revenue with shorter 6–9 month order cycles, providing better revenue visibility and scalability.

Why are we talking about it?

In July 2026, the company completed a major corporate cleanup by transitioning its loss-making European engineering services subsidiaries into judicial liquidation, permanently stopping a multi-year cash burn. This leaves a lean, highly profitable Indian core that is scaling rapidly.

Beyond defense and space, Centum is building a high-precision semiconductor equipment vertical that supplies global chip-tool makers with precision assembly components, targeting an annual sales run-rate of thirty million dollars by 2028. This vertical leverages their high-reliability manufacturing capabilities and acts as a commercial hedge against lumpy government defense procurement cycles, representing an early-stage capability bet that is scaling from a tiny base.

Despite a relatively weak Q1, management remains confident of delivering 25% revenue growth for the full year FY27. The company also expects to improve its EBITDA margin to above 13%, compared with 12.5% in the previous year, while exports are expected to contribute 50–55% of total revenue.

5. Lilly Leads, Novo Defends, the Rest Chase: The GLP-1/GIP Landscape

Good to track these names, as we are likely to hear them repeatedly in the context of Indian CDMO players!

1. Eli Lilly: Lilly leads the category. Its tirzepatide franchise (Mounjaro and Zepbound, the GLP-1/GIP dual agonist) has pushed it ahead of Novo on sales. It is now broadening into other formats. Its oral GLP-1 Foundayo is newly approved, and retatrutide, a GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist, is in Phase III. Foundayo launched in the US in April, putting it in direct competition with Novo’s pill. Lilly’s edge is that it owns the best-in-class injectable, has an oral follow-up, and has a next-generation triple agonist behind them. 

2. Novo Nordisk: Novo created the modern GLP-1 market with semaglutide but has lost ground to Lilly and is now defending its position. The Wegovy pill launched in January and drew around 1.3 million prescriptions in Q1. In Q2, though, pill sales of about DKK 3.2bn missed the 3.3bn analyst forecast, even as injectable Wegovy held strong at DKK 19.48bn. CagriSema also failed to match tirzepatide’s blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes, a setback for the main next-generation asset. Novo planned to file CagriSema in 2026 and is also developing amycretin, a GLP-1/amylin agonist, as its longer-term bet. It raised full-year guidance, though adjusted sales are still expected to decline. 

3. Amgen: Amgen is the leading large-cap challenger with a differentiated mechanism. MariTide (maridebart cafraglutide) combines GLP-1 agonism with GIP receptor antagonism, the opposite of tirzepatide’s GIP approach. It is built for monthly or less frequent dosing. Phase II data showed weight loss of up to 20% in a year, similar to Wegovy and Zepbound but with slightly more side effects. The Phase III MARITIME program is now running in obesity and related conditions such as sleep apnea and cardiovascular disease. The bet is that dosing convenience can offset a tolerability gap.

4. Viking Therapeutics: Viking Therapeutics is a prominent biotech challenger advancing VK2735, a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist designed to rival tirzepatide. The company is developing both subcutaneous (injectable) and oral formulations of VK2735 through late-stage Phase 2 and Phase 3 clinical trials, targeting substantial body weight reduction alongside favorable tolerability profiles. Viking is also exploring maintenance-dosing regimens for long-term weight management and diversifying its metabolic pipeline with complementary mechanisms like amylin agonists (VK3019).

5. Boehringer Ingelheim / Zealand Pharma: Partnering to target the broader incretin and glucagon pathways, Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma are co-developing survodutide (BI 456906), a dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist. Unlike pure GLP-1/GIP agents that focus primarily on satiety and insulin secretion, dual glucagon receptor activation increases energy expenditure and directly targets hepatic lipid metabolism. This places survodutide in a strong position for treating metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH / NASH) alongside severe obesity and Type 2 diabetes.

6. Roche (with Zealand): Roche bought its way in through two routes. CT-388 (enicepatide) is a once-weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist that came from the $2.7bn Carmot acquisition and has been advanced into late-stage trials. Roche also licensed Zealand’s amylin analogue petrelintide in a deal worth up to $5.3bn. That gives it both an incretin and an amylin asset, so it can pursue combinations later. It is the least proven of the five on commercial execution, but the pipeline is credible. 

7. Pfizer: Pfizer is the re-entrant. It had dropped two oral GLP-1 candidates, lotiglipron and danuglipron, over liver safety concerns, leaving it with no in-house obesity drug. It then bought Metsera. The main assets are MET-097i, a GLP-1 designed for monthly injection, and MET-233i, an amylin analogue. Pfizer has reported positive Phase IIb data in adults with obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes. It is still behind the field on timing, but it has the balance sheet and commercial reach to catch up. 

8. Structure Therapeutics: Structure Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing orally available, small-molecule incretin mimetics. Their lead candidate, aleniglipron (GSBR-1290), is an oral, biased GLP-1 receptor agonist engineered to deliver peptide-like efficacy without requiring complex peptide synthesis or cold-chain storage. By leveraging a small-molecule platform, Structure aims to bypass global peptide fill-finish supply bottlenecks and offer an easily accessible, cost-effective daily pill option as the market shifts toward oral formulations.

9. AstraZeneca: AstraZeneca is a late entrant that is betting on oral convenience. Elecoglipron (AZD5004) is a once-daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist that AstraZeneca licensed from Eccogene in 2023. The VISTA obesity trial and the SOLSTICE type 2 diabetes trial both met their primary endpoints, and management said the profile was competitive with other oral GLP-1s. The Phase IIb data were presented at the ADA 2026 meeting and published in The Lancet. One report put weight loss at 10.5% at 26 weeks. The drug has since moved into a global Phase III program (the Embold trials), which triggered a $50M milestone payment to Eccogene and covers obesity or overweight with and without type 2 diabetes. Beyond elecoglipron, AstraZeneca is building a wider portfolio. It includes the selective amylin agonist AZD6234, which is being tested alone and in combination with the GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist AZD9550. The main risk is timing. Lilly’s Foundayo and Novo’s Wegovy pill are already on the market, so AstraZeneca will need either a clear efficacy or tolerability edge or cheaper manufacturing to take share in the oral segment.

That's all for this edition. Have a great Sunday!

text:
Some pathways to peace from @grok double check your work and @bot how to make this function and go through for the sake of humans prosperity 

Starting with that first one. Netanyahu loses on the twenty-seventh. A new government comes in, probably led by Gadi Eisenkot or someone from the security establishment. They accept the Board of Peace framework — Hamas disarms in stages, a technocratic Palestinian authority runs civilian life, the two-point-four-five billion reconstruction package starts flowing. It gets there because Israeli voters are exhausted after three years, the economy’s been crushed by mobilization, and the hostages are all home so the emotional fuel is gone. It lasts as long as the money flows and Hamas stays bought off. The failure mode is simple: if reconstruction stalls or Hamas re-arms, you’re back to square one. It’s peace by cash flow.
Victor’s peace. One side destroys the other’s military capacity entirely — Rome after Carthage, the Allies after 1945. It gets there through overwhelming force and unconditional surrender. It lasts because the loser is occupied, re-educated, and rebuilt under the winner’s rules. The catch is it requires a level of destruction almost no modern democracy will accept, and the occupation itself breeds the next generation of resentment. It works when the victor is generous — Marshall Plan generous — and fails when it’s punitive.
Cold peace. India-Pakistan, North-South Korea. It gets there when a war ends in stalemate and both sides decide the status quo is survivable. It lasts because the cost of restarting is always higher than the cost of enduring. No love, no trust, just math. The danger is it can flip to hot war fast when a crisis hits — Kargil in ninety-nine nearly did.
Partition peace. Israel-Egypt, 1979. You give the disputed land back, demilitarize the zone, and both sides sign because each gets something concrete — Egypt got Sinai and American aid, Israel got a quiet southern border. It lasts because the deal is tangible and the enforcement is visible. Demilitarized Sinai means Egypt literally cannot attack. That’s the whole trick: make breaking the peace physically impossible.
Peace through transformation. Post-war Europe. Coal and steel — the raw materials of war — became the shared foundation of the European project. It gets there when leaders reframe the rivalry as a shared problem. It lasts because the incentive structure itself changes; fighting stops making sense. The hard part is you can’t force it. It needs a crisis big enough to make the old logic collapse and leaders bold enough to propose the new one.
And surrender dressed as peace. Gaza right now is the live case. When bakeries close and people are eating grass, “peace” means taking whatever’s offered. It gets there through starvation and siege. It doesn’t last — it just pauses until the next generation is angry enough to fight. History’s full of these: Versailles is the textbook example. The victors called it peace. Twenty years later it was a war memorial.
The pattern across all six: peace lasts when the structure makes war more expensive than peace — through money, occupation, geography, or incentives. It fails when it’s only a feeling.

text:
------ The Cursed Tale of the Hope Diamond (Kohinoor Diamond)----

The cursed history of the Koh-i-Noor diamond is widely known. Wherever it has travelled, it is said to have left a trail of destruction in its wake. Now, the story of another diamond with a similarly unfortunate reputation has come to light. In terms of its association with misfortune, it is said to be no less notorious than the Koh-i-Noor.

According to this account, about 500 years ago, someone offered this diamond at the banks of the Narmada River to be set in the crown of Lord Venkateswara. The priest was overcome by greed and stole it. When the devotees discovered the theft, they stoned him to death.

The diamond was subsequently smuggled to France. Those who possessed it reportedly became victims of misfortune. One day, they became trapped in a forest and were killed by wild dogs.

The diamond eventually came into the possession of the King of France. One day, a courtier borrowed it to wear. Shortly after leaving his home, he became the victim of a conspiracy and lost his life.

Later, the diamond came into the possession of Louis XIV, the King of France. He, too, could not wear it for long. A princess was particularly fond of wearing it, but within a short time, she became entangled in a conspiracy and was killed.

The diamond was then stolen by another person. He, too, could not enjoy its possession for long and eventually fell victim to conspirators. From there, it passed into the hands of a jeweller, who sold it for a high price. However, the buyer was also unable to retain it for long. His enemies shot him dead.

After changing hands several times, the diamond eventually reached Louis XVI, the King of France. He gave it to his wife. The two were deeply in love, but their affection supposedly came to an end following a minor quarrel. The king shot his queen dead.

A princess also wore the diamond with great delight, but she, too, reportedly lost her life in connection with a romantic affair.

The diamond subsequently came into the possession of Empress Catherine. During the political revolution of 1980, her entire family was reportedly massacred.

After being sold in one or two more transactions, the diamond finally reached a jeweller who developed a deep affection for it. He was captivated by its beauty and kept it before his eyes throughout the day. Its beauty was, indeed, extraordinary.

However, when he learned about the diamond's history, he became frightened. He arranged for it to be placed in a presidential museum in the United States, where it was kept under protection. Today, it is known as the **Hope Diamond** and is preserved in a museum.

#The Moral of the Story

The more greed, avarice, abduction, and conspiracy become associated with an object, the more it comes to be regarded as cursed by those very emotions. 

The history of the Koh-i-Noor is often described in similar terms. It is said that many of those who possessed it met untimely or violent deaths. The Hope Diamond, too, has acquired a similarly ominous reputation.

Because of their immense value, such precious objects arouse an intense desire in people to possess them. They are often not simply bought and sold; throughout history, some have been stolen or acquired through secretive and unlawful means. 

Even those who possess them are reluctant to surrender them willingly, for as long as they remain alive, they wish to retain control over what they consider their prized possession.

As conspiracies, secret agreements, and malicious intentions accumulate around an object, it may come to be regarded as cursed.

 Human beings project their negative emotions onto the objects they covet, and those objects become symbols of greed, betrayal, and misfortune. Consequently, wherever such objects travel, stories of intrigue and tragedy seem to follow.

The final jeweller acted wisely by ensuring that the diamond did not remain in the private possession of any individual but was instead entrusted to a public museum. 

In this way, the object could be preserved, while the risks associated with private rivalry and the obsessive desire to possess it could potentially be reduced.

Ultimately, it is not necessarily the object itself that brings misfortune rather, it may be the greed, possessiveness, and destructive human behaviour associated with it that create the conditions for tragedy.

text:
Being unemployed is mentally exhausting.

You wake up every day trying to stay hopeful, apply to hundreds of jobs, and still end up hearing nothing. Not even a rejection email.

Over time, the silence starts making you question your own worth.

That's why I believe we need to be kinder to people looking for jobs.

If someone reaches out to you for help, at least try to respond. You might not have a job to offer them, and that's okay. Sometimes, even a little guidance or a simple reply can make a difference.

You don't have to help everyone. You don't owe anyone a referral.

But if you can help someone without expecting anything in return, please do.

You may forget that interaction tomorrow. They might remember it for years.

In a world where everyone is fighting to get ahead, be someone who helps another person move forward.

text:
Sjoe! The Debt Has Stopped Climbing. The Leaks Are Still Having a Jol. 💸🚰😂 ~ 509 Names Flagged. Only 18 Restricted. Is the Blacklist on Annual Leave? 🏖️📋🤣 ~ Eighteen Years, One Gambling Law and a Whole Lot of “Coming Soon” 🎰⌛🤡
On 21 October 2026, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana stood in Parliament and reported that South Africa’s gross debt-to-GDP ratio had stabilised at 78.4 percent in the 2025/26 fiscal year. It was the first time the figure had stopped rising in nearly two decades (National Treasury, 2026). 

Markets responded within hours. Bonds rallied. The rand firmed. A primary surplus is now projected to approach 3 percent of GDP by the end of the decade. For a country that spent fifteen years watching its public finances erode under State Capture, repeated state-owned enterprise bailouts, chronically low growth and a pandemic, the announcement carried the weight of a long-delayed turning point.

Yet the same speech confirmed that a national tax on online gambling — an industry that has operated in a legal vacuum since Parliament passed enabling legislation in 2008 — will only reach final design in the February 2027 Budget. 

And in the same period, National Treasury could report that of 509 companies and individuals referred for restriction on the basis of Special Investigating Unit findings, only 18 had been placed on the Database of Restricted Suppliers. Four hundred and ninety-one remained under review (EWN, 2026; Democratic Alliance, 2026).

The largest fiscal leak has been slowed. The smaller, older, more humiliating ones continue to run. South Africa has bought itself time. It has not yet proved it can convert that time into the quieter work of institutional enforcement.

Sjoe!
A government that can finally make a ratio stand still still struggles to make a blacklist move. The spreadsheet is under control. The register is not.

Questions Stirring:
Does a stabilised debt ratio signal regained capacity to enforce the state’s own rules, or merely improved capacity to produce better accounts? 
If the largest leak has been slowed, why do the older ones continue at the same volume? 
What does it reveal when the same administration that can report a primary surplus still requires another year to design a tax on an industry operating in plain sight for eighteen years?

What these questions together reveal:
They test whether the 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement marks a genuine institutional turn or a temporary pause in a longer pattern of delayed enforcement. Together they separate accounting success from administrative capability, and they force attention onto the gap between what the state can measure and what it can actually stop.

1. How the Bleeding Was Slowed

Debt dynamics are unforgiving. When the interest bill grows faster than the economy and the primary balance remains in deficit, the ratio climbs almost mechanically. South Africa’s climb accelerated through the State Capture years, was sustained by low potential growth, was deepened by repeated transfers to Eskom, Transnet and other state-owned companies, and was then struck by the fiscal shock of COVID-19. 

By the mid-2020s the ratio had become the binding constraint on policy. Every new spending commitment competed with interest payments that were already absorbing a rising share of revenue.

The 2026 MTBPS presented the stabilisation at 78.4 percent as the first concrete result of earlier consolidation. A rising primary surplus and a narrowing main budget deficit were offered as evidence that spending restraint and modest revenue gains had begun to bite (National Treasury, 2026; SAnews, 2026). 

Markets treated the announcement as credible in real time. The claim of rebuilt fiscal space is therefore not rhetorical. It underpins the government’s ability to offer limited, temporary relief without immediately reversing the debt trajectory.

Yet durability remains contingent. Potential growth is still forecast at only 1.2 percent for 2026. A principles-based fiscal anchor is scheduled for legislation only in 2027. International experience shows that stabilisations achieved through temporary revenue windfalls or cyclical restraint often reverse when growth falters or political pressure for new spending returns. 

The difference between a cyclical pause and a structural repair lies less in the first year the ratio stops rising than in the subsequent years when the underlying drivers — growth, primary balance, interest costs and institutional discipline — are tested under less favourable conditions.

Sjoe!
It took nearly twenty years for the ratio to stop climbing. The markets celebrated within a single afternoon. Institutional time and market time rarely keep the same clock.

Questions Stirring:
What combination of political will and administrative capacity actually produced the change after so long a rise? 
Can a primary surplus approaching 3 percent of GDP be sustained when growth remains below 2 percent? 
Why is a formal fiscal anchor still a year away if the stabilisation is already being presented as durable?

What these questions together reveal:
They separate the achievement of a number from the capacity that produced it. A ratio that stops rising is necessary. It is not sufficient. The questions keep attention on whether the stabilisation rests on temporary conditions or on deeper changes in how the state manages its own finances.

2. Temporary Windfalls, Temporary Relief

Gross tax revenue for 2026/27 was revised upward by R17.1 billion relative to the February Budget estimate, driven largely by stronger corporate income tax, dividends tax and VAT collections linked to elevated commodity prices (Daily Maverick, 2026; Moneyweb, 2026). 

That windfall, together with non-tax revenue improvements, financed two carefully ring-fenced responses.

Temporary fuel-levy reductions — R3 per litre on diesel and R1.50 per litre on petrol from 4 November to 1 December 2026, then stepped down until early January 2027 — cost R10 billion in foregone revenue. 

At the same time the contingency reserve was increased to R10 billion, earmarked for El Niño drought response and possible further energy-price shocks. The fuel relief is financed by returning a prior R10 billion transfer from the Central Energy Fund to the National Revenue Fund rather than by permanent new spending. 

The policy logic is deliberate: earlier restraint created usable buffers that can absorb shocks without reopening the overall fiscal position. The measures are temporary and contingent by design. They preserve the credibility of the stabilisation path while offering immediate support to households and agriculture.

The arrangement is fiscally tidy. It is also revealing. A government that once transferred money out of the Central Energy Fund has now transferred it back in order to fund a short-term reduction in the fuel levy. The same rand is being used twice, once as a transfer and once as relief, without being counted as new permanent expenditure. 

Commodity prices that produced the revenue overrun are not guaranteed to remain elevated. The buffers exist because of favourable conditions and prior restraint. Whether they can be replenished under less favourable conditions remains an open test of the stabilisation’s depth.

Sjoe!
The state has learned to recycle its own transfers with impressive efficiency. Whether it has learned to live without the next commodity upswing is a different and harder lesson.

Questions Stirring:
If temporary buffers can be created by recycling earlier transfers, what happens when the next commodity cycle turns down? 
Does a contingency reserve of R10 billion represent genuine preparedness for a severe El Niño, or simply the residual of a revenue overrun? 
How long can temporary measures remain temporary before they become politically permanent?

What these questions together reveal:
They probe the difference between buffers created by favourable prices and buffers created by structural capacity. Temporary measures are appropriate. The open question is whether the underlying fiscal and administrative machinery is being strengthened so that temporary measures do not become the permanent mode of governance.

3. The Eighteen-Year Vacuum

In 2008 Parliament passed the National Gambling Amendment Act, intended to create a regulatory framework for interactive — online — gambling. The Act was never brought into force. In the resulting vacuum the online market expanded rapidly. Industry estimates indicate that a substantial share of activity, and more than R50 billion in annual gross gambling revenue, has flowed to offshore or illegal operators that pay little or no South African tax and operate under weaker auditing and player-protection standards than licensed local operators (Daily Investor, 2026; BusinessTech, 2026).

In the 2026 MTBPS, Treasury confirmed that a National Online Gambling Tax — proposed at 20 percent of gross gambling revenue from online betting and interactive gambling, additional to existing provincial taxes — remains under design. 

The final architecture is scheduled for announcement in the February 2027 Budget. Consultations continue on linkages to the existing regulatory framework and implications for provinces.

Eighteen years after legislation was passed, the state is still designing the tax. The industry did not wait. Money left the formal tax base. Player-protection standards remained uneven. The regulatory gap became one more example of known problems meeting delayed follow-through. 

The parallel with other long-standing institutional gaps is difficult to ignore. A government that can stabilise a debt ratio in a single fiscal year still requires another full year merely to complete the design of a tax on an industry that has operated in plain sight since the Act was first passed.

Political science offers a familiar pattern: legislation that creates concentrated costs for organised interests and diffuse benefits for the public often stalls in implementation. The longer the delay, the larger the vested interests that grow inside the vacuum, and the harder the eventual reform becomes. 

South Africa’s online gambling experience fits the pattern with uncomfortable precision.

Sjoe!
An Act can be passed in a single year. Proclaiming it, it turns out, can take the better part of a generation. The market, meanwhile, kept its own schedule.

Questions Stirring:
Why did an Act passed in 2008 remain unproclaimed for eighteen years while the market it was meant to regulate grew into a multi-billion-rand sector? 
If a 20 percent national tax is now under design, what enforcement capacity will accompany it, and will that capacity reach the offshore operators that currently capture the largest share of the revenue? 
How many other pieces of legislation sit in the same state of suspended animation?

What these questions together reveal:
They expose the difference between announcing a repair and completing one. Fiscal stabilisation addresses the largest visible leak. The gambling vacuum is one of the older, quieter ones that continued to run while attention was elsewhere. The questions keep the focus on implementation capacity rather than legislative intention.

4. The Blacklist That Will Not Fill

Around September 2025 the Presidency, drawing on Special Investigating Unit findings, referred 509 companies and individuals to National Treasury for possible restriction. By late September 2026 only 18 had been placed on the Database of Restricted Suppliers.  Four hundred and ninety-one remained under review (EWN, 2026; Rio Times, 2026).

Finance Minister Godongwana has repeatedly stated that Treasury cannot act unilaterally. The contracting organ of state must initiate the process, afford the supplier an opportunity to respond, and submit complete documentation. Major entities including Eskom, Transnet and the Umngeni Water Board have been slow or non-responsive. 

The older 2004 Register for Tender Defaulters remains empty. High-profile cases such as the R2 billion Tembisa Hospital procurement — 207 suppliers, none restricted — illustrate the practical consequence.

In response, the Democratic Alliance launched its Blacklist Project online whistle-blower portal on 14 October 2026, allowing the public to submit information about companies and individuals suspected of abusing public procurement (Democratic Alliance, 2026). ActionSA has tabled legislation seeking mandatory timelines and Treasury step-in powers. 

The official registers stay largely empty while opposition parties build parallel systems to force the process forward.

The pattern is institutional rather than accidental. Known problems. Documented referrals. Incomplete administrative follow-through. The same week the debt-to-GDP ratio was reported as stabilised, 491 entities flagged for possible restriction remained free to bid for state contracts. 

When formal systems move slowly, informal and opposition systems emerge to fill the gap. That emergence is itself evidence of where enforcement pressure now has to come from.

Sjoe!
Five hundred and nine referrals. Eighteen restrictions. The arithmetic is almost elegant in its refusal to hurry.

Questions Stirring:
If 509 referrals produce only 18 actual restrictions after a full year, what does that ratio reveal about the administrative capacity of the organs of state that are supposed to initiate the process? 
Why does the 2004 Register for Tender Defaulters remain empty more than two decades after it was created? 
When opposition parties are reduced to launching public portals because the official databases do not move, what does that say about where enforcement pressure now originates?

What these questions together reveal:
They move the diagnosis from delayed regulation to active non-enforcement. A stabilised debt ratio can coexist with a procurement system that still struggles to remove known high-risk suppliers from the bidding pool. The questions keep attention on the gap between referral and consequence.

5. The Claim of a Turn, Still Unproven

After approximately fifteen years of economic under-performance, rising debt and regulatory paralysis, the 2026 MTBPS frames debt stabilisation, temporary relief measures, infrastructure financing reforms and the advancing online-gambling tax as elements of a single narrative: the state is beginning to close both large fiscal leaks and smaller persistent ones. 

Parallel external pressure — most visibly the DA’s Blacklist Project portal and ActionSA’s legislative efforts — adds public and parliamentary cost to continued inaction on supplier restrictions.

The significance is diagnostic rather than conclusive. Success will ultimately be measured not solely by debt ratios or primary-surplus targets, but by whether long-delayed reforms produce tangible results within defined time frames: remote-gambling licensing and enforcement, measurable reductions in municipal non-revenue water, improved grant integrity, and actual loading of restricted suppliers onto the official database.

The mini-budget is therefore best read less as a finished achievement and more as a testable claim of institutional recovery. The largest leak has been slowed. The older ones remain open. The country has bought itself time. The institutions that spent fifteen years creating many of those leaks have not yet demonstrated that they can close them.

International comparisons sharpen the point. Several emerging economies have stabilised debt ratios only to see them resume climbing when growth disappointed or political pressure for spending returned. The difference between a pause and a repair lies in whether the underlying administrative and political incentives change. 

South Africa’s test is whether the same state that can produce a primary surplus can also enforce its own procurement rules, regulate a market it has left unregulated for eighteen years, and convert temporary buffers into lasting capacity.

Sjoe!
The patient has stopped losing blood at the previous rate. The older wounds are still open. Recovery is declared. The drains are still being watched.

Questions Stirring:
If the 2026 MTBPS is a claim of a turn, what concrete metrics — beyond the debt ratio — will be used to test whether the claim holds by the time of the 2027 Budget? 
When does a temporary contingency reserve become evidence of preparedness rather than residual accounting? 
How many more years of “under review” status for referred suppliers will be required before the system is judged to have failed rather than merely delayed?

What these questions together reveal:
They refuse to let the headline number stand alone. They insist that institutional recovery is measured by enforcement outcomes, not only by stabilisation statistics. Together they keep the diagnostic focus on whether time purchased through fiscal discipline is being used to close the remaining leaks.

Synthesis: The Weight of Converging Evidence

The evidence forms a coherent pattern across fiscal accounts, legislative history and administrative performance. 
Debt-to-GDP stabilisation at 78.4 percent after nearly two decades is real and market-recognised (National Treasury, 2026; News24, 2026). 
Temporary buffers financed by revenue overruns and recycled transfers are real and deliberately ring-fenced (Daily Maverick, 2026). 
An eighteen-year vacuum in online-gambling regulation is real and only now moving toward a tax design scheduled for 2027 (Daily Investor, 2026). 
An 18-of-509 restriction rate on referred suppliers is real and documented in parliamentary replies (EWN, 2026). 
Opposition portals and private-member bills are real responses to official inertia (Democratic Alliance, 2026).

Taken together, the converging lines of evidence show a state that has slowed the largest fiscal leak while the smaller, older ones continue to run. 

The argument is falsifiable. If the February 2027 Budget delivers an enforceable online-gambling tax with clear reach to offshore operators, if the Database of Restricted Suppliers begins to fill at a measurable rate, and if non-revenue water and grant-integrity metrics improve within defined periods, the claim of a turn strengthens. 

If those indicators remain flat, the stabilisation of the debt ratio will stand as an accounting success that did not translate into broader institutional repair.

The stakes are straightforward. South Africa has purchased time with fiscal discipline. Whether that time is used to close the remaining leaks will determine whether the incomplete repair becomes a completed one.

Objections

One objection holds that debt stabilisation itself is the decisive achievement and that secondary issues such as gambling regulation and supplier blacklisting are lower-order problems. The response is that the same speech that announced the stabilisation also confirmed the continued delay on the gambling tax and occurred in the same period as the 18-of-509 restriction rate. The issues are linked by the same pattern of delayed enforcement.

A second objection notes that Treasury cannot act unilaterally on restrictions and that the fault lies with the contracting organs of state. The response is that this explanation has been offered for years while the 2004 Register remains empty and the 2025 referrals remain largely unresolved. An explanation that produces the same outcome year after year eventually becomes part of the problem it describes.

A third objection argues that temporary measures are appropriate given remaining fiscal risks. The response is that temporary measures are indeed appropriate; the open question is whether the underlying administrative capacity is being strengthened so that temporary measures do not become the permanent mode of governance.

Conclusion

South Africa has achieved the first stabilisation of its debt-to-GDP ratio in nearly twenty years and has used the resulting space for temporary, carefully ring-fenced relief. That is not nothing. It is also not enough. 

The same week the numbers improved, 491 companies flagged for possible restriction remained free to bid for state contracts, an eighteen-year-old gambling law remained unproclaimed, and opposition parties were reduced to launching public portals because the official registers stay empty.

The incomplete repair is therefore both real and unfinished. 

The country has bought itself time. The only question that still matters is whether the institutions that spent fifteen years creating many of the leaks can now be made to close them.

The cumulative weight of independent evidence — fiscal accounts, legislative timelines, administrative performance data and contemporaneous market and political responses — shows that stabilisation has occurred while the deeper work of institutional enforcement remains incomplete.

text:
"Obituary for Frederick (Fred) Mann
In 5,4,3,2,1, cue talent…

We have some sad news to report today about the passing of a beloved professor of communications. Frederick (Fred) Mann passed away in McAllen, Texas, on March 28, 2026, at the age of 76.
Born to Winne and Fred Mann in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 7, 1949, Fred was the oldest of three children and had a nomadic childhood due to his father’s Coast Guard stateside career. After attending schools in Ohio, Michigan and Louisiana, Fred graduated from Churchland High School in Virginia. Shortly after graduating, the family moved to Texas where Fred attended Texas A&I University in Kingsville. He met Virginia Villarreal there, and the two were married in 1970.

After receiving their Bachelor’s Degrees in Education, Fred and Virginia moved to McAllen and Fred began serving in the U.S. Army National Guard and later in the U.S. Army Reserve. He served for over 20 years during tumultuous times and was never called up nor saw combat, retiring as an Infantry Major. Fred credited his great-grandfather Samuel White, who was imprisoned during the Civil War, as being his guardian angel.

In 1972, Fred began teaching at McAllen ISD – a career that spanned 30 years. His first teaching assignment was World History at Lincoln Junior High, where he also took care of the audio-visual equipment, mostly 16mm and overhead projectors. Having loved radios from a young age, Fred began a student radio club, KLIN, which played music into the cafeteria during lunch periods. This became his inspiration to develop a course in Radio & Television production for the district.

Fred received his Master’s Degree from East Texas State University in Educational Technology and began teaching classes in Radio and TV Production. Instruction focused on hands-on, real-life experiences such as taping sporting events, performing DJ work at school functions, producing weekly news programs, and interviewing local and national celebrities such as George Bush, Laura Bush, Jesse Jackson and Miss USA Laura Martinez Herring. Fred’s high school students went on to win numerous state and national awards. The students were even asked to stop participating in one national contest because, as high school students, they were winning many of the categories and the contest was meant for university radio/TV programs.

Fred would beam with pride when his students won national recognition for their productions. He was especially proud of their winning the Pacemaker Award for Best Television Newscast Nationwide, CNN-Student Bureau, 1st Place Award in Sports, Channel One, #1 Newscast in the Nation, and the airing of a CNN-Student Bureau story televised on CNN Newsroom worldwide. In 2002, Fred received the All-American Adviser Award presented by the National Scholastic Press Association.

A highlight of his career was participating in the People to People Citizen Ambassador Program to Viet Nam in 1993. The 12-member Visual Literacy Delegation spent two weeks touring schools in Viet Nam, participating in panel discussions and meeting with professional counterparts to discuss visual media in their respective classrooms.

After retiring from McAllen ISD in 2002, a chance encounter with Dr. Marian Monta opened a brand-new opportunity for Fred to teach a television production class at the University of Texas Pan American. From adjunct to full-time professor, Fred loved his 15 years as an educator at the university. He worked with an amazing, dedicated team of professors in the communications department and soon began leaving his mark. He started Bronc Radio and Bronc TV, where students could refine their on-air skills and put into practice all the facets involved in producing weekly news programs. They entered contests and brought home as many as 15 awards in one year from the Texas Intercollegiate Press Association. Fred helped many of his students get internships at local stations, and numerous students were offered positions when their internships were completed. He retired from UTRGV in 2018.

Having been raised in a Coast Guard family, in 2005 Fred joined the Coast Guard Auxiliary Flotilla at South Padre Island. This volunteer organization supports the U.S. Coast Guard, focusing on boat inspections, recreational Boating Safety Classes, and public information. Fred served for 15 years, using his media skills to become a Public Affairs Specialist, and received numerous commendations and awards for his service.

Fred and Virginia loved to travel, doing most of their traveling from the 1970’s through 2015. They enjoyed camping in their VW Vanagon and later in their Toyota Chinook. Their travels took them throughout the U.S., Mexico, and Canada. Fred’s favorite national park was Big Bend National Park in Texas. Fred and Virginia made many trips to the remote park, and Fred proudly served on the Board of Directors of the Friends of Big Bend in 2003-2005.

When it came to favorite pastimes, Fred spent countless hours on his ham radios. Known to his ham radio friends as N5IVZ, he collected QSL cards from ham operators around the world and was proud of his “Worked All States” and “Worked All Continents” Awards using Morse Code. He also enjoyed riding his bicycle and even competed in the Chihuahuan Desert Mountain Bike Challenge in Lajitas, Texas, in 2000. Arriving at the finish line scraped, bloodied, bruised, and grinning from ear to ear, Fred told Virginia, “Wow! That was a kick!” Fred continued riding until his Parkinson’s disease diagnosis in 2016.

For the last 10 years of his life, Fred faced declining physical and mental health which required more and more assistance. He lived at Waterford Gardens for two years and at Avalon Memory Care until his death on March 28, 2026. During this time, he and Virginia met many an angel on earth who lovingly cared for him and met his every need. Eric, Fred’s younger brother, died in December 2025. They are now together again either reading, playing chess (Eric’s choice) or Battleship (Fred’s favorite).

After hearing of Fred’s passing, friends and family flooded Facebook with an outpouring of love. Students shared personal accounts about their beloved teacher, Mr. Mann, and how his mentoring, support, and encouragement forever changed the course of their lives and inspired them to believe in themselves.

Fred is survived by his wife of 55 years, Virginia Villarreal Mann. He is also survived by his sister Victoria Mann Bolling (Rick) of Auburn, Alabama, his sister’s five children and five grandchildren, and numerous cousins.

Info: Bottom line: The piece is sourced investigative work drawing on public documents and archives rather than unattributed AI generation. Core factual claims about the privacy policy change, Twilio, company location/history near Fort Meade, founders’ backgrounds, Shawn’s co-founder role, and call-record retention are supported by available public records. Interpretations of motive, the weight of the “scrubbed past,” and how alarming the retention practices are relative to industry norms are the parts most open to debate. Full independent verification of every archive snapshot and minor detail would require checking the Wayback links directly.The deep dive (“GLACIER: THE PRIVACY APP WITH A PAST IT ERASED,” by Leah /@theleahfiles, Oct 20, 2026) is primarily document- and archive-based investigative writing, not pure AI-generated research. It cites specific Wayback Machine captures, company privacy policies and versions by date, press releases, USPTO filings, USASpending data, App Store listings, GitHub history, and public bios. The style is polished and narrative (common on Substack), and AI tools could have been used for drafting or organization, but the core claims rest on primary sources that can be checked. Leah has stated she ran the work by tech experts. Candace Owens has broadly labeled Leah’s research “shoddy AI” in the context of their dispute, but this specific piece is heavily sourced rather than generic AI output.substack.comKey claims that check out or are supported by public records
Privacy policy evolution: Earlier versions (around mid-June 2026) used broad “does not store, retain, or archive any logs” language. Later versions (around the July 24, 2026 launch window and after) narrowed the no-logs promise to DNS/VPN activity and added an explicit Phone & Calling Data section that collects call metadata (numbers, timestamps, duration) and voicemail audio, retained as needed for the feature and tied to the account. Twilio is listed as the processor for number provisioning, calling, and voicemail. The live policy matches this. Archives support the timing of changes.theglacierapp.comTwilio involvement: Confirmed as the underlying carrier for the “burner” numbers. Twilio publishes transparency data on government requests (high compliance rates are public).
Company structure and history: Glacier Security (Maryland, Annapolis Junction / near Fort Meade / National Business Park) was founded around 2015 by people with intelligence/cyber backgrounds. Alex White is the publicly identified former NSA engineer and CTO. Shawn Ryan is listed as co-founder of Security App LLC (the consumer-facing entity) in press materials. The consumer app launched in 2026; prior products existed (chat, dial, etc.). Website content referencing the Fort Meade-area location and certain bios/history was altered or removed in the period leading into the consumer launch (archives document this).
Shawn Ryan’s role: He promoted the app on his show (including “Shawn built Glacier”-style language) and is a co-founder of the selling entity. Ownership stake size is not fully public.
What the article does not claim: Leah explicitly states there is no evidence Glacier sells user data. She focuses on policy language, retention of call records/voicemail, the company’s prior government/enterprise work and location, scrubbed site content, and lack of a transparency report or clear subpoena language compared with Signal, Proton, or Mullvad.
Nuances, interpretive elements, or points that have been contested“HQ Fort Meade” and intel contractor framing: The physical address is in Annapolis Junction (near NSA headquarters). Older site versions listed it in ways that invoked the Fort Meade area; this was later de-emphasized. The company did government/enterprise and high-risk client work. Framing it as a decade of selling primarily to the intelligence world is directionally true given founders and location but overstates the scale of direct prime federal contracting (the article itself notes modest subcontract revenue).
CEO bio details: The piece attributes a résumé mentioning telecommunications exploitation and automated data exfiltration to the CEO (named in archives as Lemuel Riggins). Alex White is the more visible former NSA figure. The bio was on the site and later removed, per archives.
Policy change significance: Changing language after launch (and the gap between marketing “privacy” claims and actual call-record retention) is factually documented. Whether this is deceptive, merely reflecting the addition of calling features, or standard for a phone-number provider is interpretive. Call metadata and voicemail retention by the service provider (and underlying carrier) is common and often required for service delivery and legal compliance; subpoenas typically go to Twilio as the number owner.
Broader implications: The piece is careful not to allege active data selling or NSA/Mossad-style collusion. Stronger conspiracy-tinged readings (Shawn colluding to steal data, etc.) come from surrounding commentary rather than the article’s text itself. Candace Owens has said parts of Leah’s Glacier-related work contain “obvious errors” and that some of what was framed as conspiracy is ordinary federal compliance.

text:
AgentVQA: a unified offline benchmark for agentic visual understanding - and the best VLM only reaches 58.5%

Online agent evaluations in simulators are costly and hard to scale. AgentVQA (arXiv 2610.31494, U Maryland + Princeton) offers an offline proxy that tracks online rankings: 1,000 manually selected challenging examples from 23 source datasets across five agent domains - Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, Spatial Planning - tested on 22 VLMs.

Results: the best model averages only 58.5%. Domain averages show where agents stand: Egocentric Videos 59%, Games 51.5%, Spatial Planning 46%, Robotics 38%, Web Agents 29% - web is hardest, with only three models above 40%. Per-domain leaders differ: Qwen3.7 Flash leads Egocentric Videos (72.5%), Gemini 3.7 Flash leads Games (70%), Spatial Planning (62.5%) and Robotics (52.5%), GPT-5.6-sol thinking-high leads Web Agents (47%). Games shows the widest spread (23-70%). Error analysis points to visual-state grounding - localizing UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes, inferring 3D relations - rather than task misinterpretation or logical reasoning; 78% of analyzed web-agent errors were grounding failures. Removing action history costs ~10 points on web tasks.

These are the authors' reported results.

Source: https://t.co/Ih7ErjyPBx

Justin Bieber เปิดตัวประสบการณ์ฟังเพลง Immersive Audio ครั้งแรกของ SKYLRK ที่กรุงโซล ประเทศเกาหลีใต้ โดยเป็นผลงานที่เจ้าตัวออกแบบและโปรดิวซ์ด้วยตัวเอง เพื่อสร้างประสบการณ์การฟังเพลงรูปแบบใหม่ที่ผสมผสานเสียงเข้ากับพื้นที่ทางสถาปัตยกรรมและองค์ประกอบทางภาพ พร้อมลำโพง SKYLRK AUDIO ที่ออกแบบขึ้นเป็นพิเศษ เปลี่ยนการฟังเพลงแบบเดิมให้กลายเป็นประสบการณ์ที่ผู้คนสามารถสัมผัสร่วมกันได้

โปรเจกต์นี้ถือเป็น Experiential Installation ครั้งแรกของ Bieber ที่มุ่งเน้นเทคโนโลยี Spatial Audio หรือระบบเสียงเชิงพื้นที่ พร้อมแนะนำระบบนิเวศผลิตภัณฑ์ SKYLRK AUDIO ที่กำลังขยายตัว และสำรวจแนวทางสร้างสรรค์ใหม่ๆ นอกเหนือจากการปล่อยผลงานเพลงตามปกติ

นอกจากนี้ พื้นที่จัดงานยังเผยโฉมคอลเล็กชั่นอุปกรณ์ที่เตรียมเปิดตัวในอนาคต ซึ่งเป็นความร่วมมือระหว่าง SKYLRK และ STIGA Table Tennis โดยประกอบด้วยโต๊ะปิงปองสั่งทำพิเศษและอุปกรณ์ที่ออกแบบให้เข้าชุดกัน ถ่ายทอดแนวทางการออกแบบของแบรนด์สู่กิจกรรมสันทนาการที่ผู้คนสามารถมีส่วนร่วมร่วมกันได้

การจัดงานครั้งนี้นับเป็นการเปิดพื้นที่จริงครั้งที่ 4 ของ SKYLRK ต่อจากโตเกียวในเดือนธันวาคม 2025, อินดิโอ รัฐแคลิฟอร์เนีย ในเดือนเมษายน 2026 และนิวยอร์กซิตี้ในเดือนกรกฎาคม 2026

SKYLRK SEOUL เปิดให้เข้าชมระหว่างวันที่ 23 ถึง 25 ตุลาคม 2026 เวลา 10.00 ถึง 22.00 น. ณ 36 Seongsuil-ro 6-gil, Seongdong-gu กรุงโซล ประเทศเกาหลีใต้
-
Justin Bieber has unveiled SKYLRK’s first immersive audio experience in Seoul, South Korea. Personally conceived and produced by Bieber, the installation offers a new way to experience music by combining sound, architectural space, visual elements, and specially designed SKYLRK AUDIO speakers, transforming traditional listening into a shared, multisensory experience.

The project marks Bieber’s first experiential installation focused on spatial audio technology. It also introduces the expanding SKYLRK AUDIO ecosystem while exploring new creative possibilities beyond conventional music releases.

The space also offers a preview of an upcoming equipment collection created in collaboration with STIGA Table Tennis. The collection features custom-designed ping pong tables and matching gear, bringing SKYLRK’s design ethos into the world of communal recreation.

The Seoul installation marks SKYLRK’s fourth physical activation, following previous installations in Tokyo in December 2025, Indio, California, in April 2026, and New York City in July 2026.

SKYLRK SEOUL runs from October 23 to 25, 2026, from 10 AM to 10 PM daily at 36 Seongsuil-ro 6-gil, Seongdong-gu, Seoul, South Korea.
