👈 مصاحبه ماریو نوفال (@MarioNawfal) با پروفسور دیوید ان. گیبس (@DavidNGibbs)، استاد تاریخ و علوم سیاسی دانشگاه آریزونا. او دارای دکتری علوم سیاسی از MIT است و آثار مهمی درباره سیاست خارجی آمریکا، مداخلات بشردوستانه و اقتصاد سیاسی نوشته است؛ از جمله کتاب‌های «اول آسیب نرسان: مداخله بشردوستانه و نابودی یوگسلاوی» و «شورش ثروتمندان: چگونه سیاست‌های دهه ۱۹۷۰ شکاف طبقاتی آمریکا را عمیق‌تر کرد».

✅ ۱ – ادعاها
🔺۱.۱: ترامپ هیچ مسیر روشنی به سمت چیزی که بتواند آن را پیروزی بنامد ندارد و ادامه یا تشدید جنگ بیشتر شبیه واکنش ناامیدانه است.
🔺۱.۲: ریسک استفاده از سلاح هسته‌ای با ادامه تشدید افزایش می‌یابد و این خطر واقعی است.
🔺۱.۳: حمله آمریکا و اسرائیل منطق طرفداران ساخت سلاح هسته‌ای در داخل ایران را تقویت کرده و احتمال حرکت ایران به سمت آن را بیشتر کرده است.
🔺۱.۴: بهترین گزینه پذیرش تحقیر و خروج از جنگ است، چون تحقیر شخصی از ویرانی گسترده و ریسک هسته‌ای بسیار کمتر است.
🔺۱.۵: جنگ عدم‌قطعیت شدید اقتصادی ایجاد کرده که در کنار جنگ اوکراین و بی‌ثباتی سیاسی غرب، خطر بروز بحران بزرگ اقتصادی را بالا می‌برد.

✅ ۲ – استدلال‌ها
🔺۲.۱: پس از آغاز جنگ، خروج برای ترامپ به معنای پذیرش شکست و تحقیر است. مشابه ویتنام، جایی که جانسون پس از تشدید دیگر نمی‌توانست خارج شود چون خروج معادل شکست بود. ترامپ نیز برای جلوگیری از تحقیر به تشدید متمایل است و هیچ راه خروج آبرومندانه‌ای ندارد.
🔺۲.۲: حمله به رهبری ایران و ترور مقامات ارشد جعبه پاندورا را گشوده است. وقتی یک طرف به ترور رهبران دست می‌زند، طرف مقابل نیز ممکن است به همان روش متوسل شود. تهدید به حمله به دیمونا، ترور مقامات آمریکایی یا تخریب زیرساخت‌ها در شرایط ناامیدی محتمل است و چنین تشدیدی می‌تواند به پاسخ هسته‌ای اسرائیل منجر شود.
🔺۲.۳: منطق سخت‌گیران ایرانی این است که کره شمالی با داشتن سلاح هسته‌ای مورد حمله قرار نگرفت و قذافی با کنار گذاشتن برنامه هسته‌ای سرنگون شد. ادامه حملات این استدلال را تقویت می‌کند و میانه‌روها را تضعیف می‌کند.
🔺۲.۴: چتر امنیتی آمریکا در خلیج فارس شکست خورده است. وجود پایگاه‌ها به جای ایجاد امنیت، کشور میزبان را هدف حمله قرار داده و آمریکا نتوانسته از تخریب زیرساخت‌ها جلوگیری کند. این تجربه جذابیت هم‌پیمانی با آمریکا را کاهش می‌دهد.
🔺۲.۵: ترامپ تجربه دیپلماتیک کمی دارد و کنترل عاطفی‌اش ضعیف است. او پیام‌رسانان خبر بد را حذف کرده و مشاورانی که نظر مخالف داده‌اند را کنار گذاشته است. این محیط تصمیم‌گیری احتمال خطاهای محاسباتی را افزایش می‌دهد.

✅ ۳ – شواهد و قرائن
🔺۳.۱: پیش از آغاز جنگ، تاکر کارلسون شخصاً به ترامپ هشدار داد که جنگ ریاست‌جمهوری‌اش را نابود خواهد کرد. ترامپ مخالفت نکرد اما پاسخ داد «همه ما بالاخره می‌میریم». این پاسخ نشان‌دهنده تصمیم از پیش گرفته‌شده و نگرش نگران‌کننده است.
🔺۳.۲: آمریکا بخش عمده موشک‌های رهگیر خود را مصرف کرده و با وجود بودجه نظامی عظیم نتوانسته تنگه هرمز را باز نگه دارد یا تهدید حوثی‌ها را مهار کند. ذخایر مهمات کلیدی به شدت کاهش یافته است.
🔺۳.۳: بسیاری از افراد نزدیک به ترامپ، حتی برخی که معمولاً جنگ‌طلب تلقی می‌شوند، با ادامه جنگ مخالف‌اند اما او به آن‌ها گوش نمی‌دهد و فضای اطرافش به‌گونه‌ای است که افراد از انتقال اخبار بد خودداری می‌کنند.
🔺۳.۴: افزایش قیمت سوخت و فشار اقتصادی ناشی از جنگ، اعتراضات خیابانی در فرانسه، ایتالیا و دیگر کشورهای اروپایی را تشدید کرده است. کشورهای خلیج فارس نیز از وضعیت امنیتی خود ناراضی‌اند.
🔺۳.۵: ایران تاکنون از حمله مستقیم به دیمونا خودداری کرده اما تهدید به چنین حمله‌ای مطرح شده است. همزمان گزارش‌هایی از تهدید علیه مقامات آمریکایی و زیرساخت‌های حیاتی وجود دارد.

✅ ۴ – نتایج
🔺۴.۱: هیچ مسیری وجود ندارد که ترامپ بتواند از طریق تشدید نظامی چیزی را که پیروزی بنامد به دست آورد. ادامه جنگ تنها ویرانی بیشتر به بار می‌آورد.
🔺۴.۲: هرچه تشدید بیشتر شود، احتمال استفاده از سلاح هسته‌ای توسط اسرائیل یا آمریکا و نیز حرکت ایران به سمت ساخت سلاح هسته‌ای افزایش می‌یابد. این یکی از میراث‌های اصلی حمله اولیه است.
🔺۴.۳: بهترین گزینه پذیرش تحقیر و خروج از جنگ است. با این حال بعید است که او این مسیر را انتخاب کند.
🔺۴.۴: آمریکا در حال از دست دادن اعتبار به‌عنوان تضمین‌کننده امنیت است و نفوذ جهانی‌اش کاهش می‌یابد. در مقابل چین به نظر می‌رسد به دنبال کاهش تنش‌ها و حفظ ثبات است.
🔺۴.۵: محیط تصمیم‌گیری اطراف ترامپ مستعد خطای محاسباتی و واکنش‌های احساسی است و این وضعیت خطر تصمیمات فاجعه‌بار را بالا برده است.

Let me analyze this parlay 🏆🤑

🧩 1. Trey McBride — Anytime touchdown (+130)
Denver Broncos @ Arizona Cardinals
+130
Implied probability: 43.5%
✅ Advantages
🎯 McBride can be a major receiving target, including on short passes near the goal line.
🏈 His ability to gain yards after the catch gives Arizona another way to create scoring opportunities.
📈 If Arizona reaches the red zone multiple times, he could have more than one chance to score.
⚠️ Risks
🔄 Other Cardinals receivers and running backs can take the touchdown opportunities.
🛡️ Denver's defense may limit Arizona's passing efficiency.
📉 A strong receiving performance doesn't automatically translate into a touchdown.
Verdict: 🟢 One of the more appealing legs. McBride has a plausible path to the end zone, especially if Arizona generates several scoring drives.
🧩 2. Tucker Kraft — Anytime touchdown (+175)
Green Bay Packers @ Detroit Lions
+175
Implied probability: 36.4%
✅ Advantages
🎯 Kraft can be a receiving option on short passes and red-zone plays.
🏈 His tight-end position can create mismatches against linebackers and safeties.
📈 A competitive game with several Green Bay scoring drives could give him multiple opportunities.
⚠️ Risks
🔄 Green Bay has other receiving targets and running backs who can score instead.
🛡️ Detroit could limit his opportunities near the goal line.
📉 Kraft might gain receiving yards without scoring a touchdown.
Verdict: 🟡 A reasonable long-shot selection. The +175 odds offer an appealing payout, but Kraft needs a touchdown rather than simply a productive receiving game.
🧩 3. Brock Bowers — Anytime touchdown (+110)
Los Angeles Rams @ Las Vegas Raiders
+110
Implied probability: 47.6%
✅ Advantages
🎯 Bowers can create scoring opportunities through short receptions and yards after the catch.
🏈 His receiving role gives him multiple possible routes to the end zone.
📈 If Las Vegas sustains drives, he could receive opportunities in the red zone.
⚠️ Risks
🔄 Other Raiders receivers and running backs may take the scoring opportunities.
🛡️ The Rams could focus coverage on Bowers.
🚨 He can have a productive game without scoring, particularly if the Raiders finish drives through rushing touchdowns.
Verdict: 🟢 My preferred leg based on the displayed odds. Bowers has an appealing route to a touchdown, but +110 still represents a near-even-money proposition rather than a guarantee.

Tampa Bay History Center, military tickets on the Riverwalk

What: three floors of Florida history at 801 Water Street along the Tampa Riverwalk, from conquistadors and cattle ranchers to the Touchton Map Library. Current exhibits include Cinema in the Sunshine State and Mapping the 14th Colony, and the Columbia Cafe inside serves Spanish and Cuban dishes from the original Ybor City restaurant.

The military offer: active military and veterans get discounted tickets with ID. The center does not list the amount on its visit page, so ask at the counter.

Who and how: the discount is handled at Visitor Services on the second floor, so bring your military or veteran ID. The museum is open daily from 10 AM to 5 PM. Families with a SNAP EBT card and photo ID get free admission for the cardholder plus three guests, and library passes from Hillsborough, Pasco, Pinellas and Hernando county libraries also unlock free entry.

Sources: Tampa Bay History Center plan your visit page.

Glazer Children's Museum, 20% off for active military

What: a hands on children's museum at 110 West Gasparilla Plaza in downtown Tampa. Spooky Science runs through Sat Oct 31 with mad scientist STEAM activities, not so spooky storytimes and live science shows, and on Sun Nov 1 the Gingerbread Village opens, where families design and build a growing village from recycled materials, included with admission.

The military offer: active military get 20% off admission, a discount the museum also gives first responders, teachers and seniors over 65. General admission is $27.95, Florida residents pay $22.95 with a Florida ID, and babies under 1 play free.

text:
A Major Drug Breakthrough Could Change How Ozempic and Wegovy Work | Duke University, SciTechDaily

New compounds have overcome a longstanding challenge by directly targeting β-arrestins, proteins that regulate cellular signals, providing laboratory tools that could help guide more precise treatments with fewer side effects.

A drug can hit its intended target and still have its effects cut short. That’s because cells have built-in molecular brakes that dial down signals after a receptor is activated. Now, scientists have discovered a way to interfere with those brakes, keeping an important signaling pathway active longer at the same receptor targeted by the blockbuster weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy.

The breakthrough involves three new drug-like molecules that block β-arrestins, proteins that normally dampen cellular signals. In laboratory experiments, the compounds prolonged signaling without directly targeting the GLP-1 receptor, opening a potential path toward more precise medicines with fewer side effects.

Decades ago, Duke University biochemist and cardiologist Robert J. Lefkowitz, MD, and his colleagues discovered those regulatory proteins, called β-arrestins. Now, work from his laboratory, published in Nature, gives scientists their first chemical tools for directly controlling β-arrestins and investigating how they shape cellular responses.

β-Arrestins restrain some signals and trigger others

β-Arrestins help regulate G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs, the family that includes the GLP-1 receptor. Nearly every human cell depends on GPCRs to receive and send signals for normal function, and roughly one-third of all FDA-approved drugs target them. When these receptors become active, G proteins relay their signals within the cell. β-Arrestins can limit the response by attaching to the receptors, dampening their signaling, and drawing them inside the cell.

In the early 2000s, the Lefkowitz lab established that β-arrestins also initiate signaling pathways of their own. That discovery revealed two distinct roles for the proteins, restraining signals carried by G proteins while setting other cellular responses in motion. The new compounds let researchers interfere directly with both β-arrestin functions while preserving G protein signaling.

Blocking β-arrestins preserves G protein signaling

Finding and understanding these molecules took more than a decade of work by co-first authors Alem W. Kahsai, PhD, an assistant professor of medicine, and Natalia Pakharukova, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher. Lefkowitz said Kahsai “lived and breathed” the molecules 24 hours a day, bringing together collaborators from Duke and across the country to “describe an extraordinary amount of their biology.”

The search started with a broad, unbiased screen of the National Cancer Institute’s extensive compound library. Researchers looked for molecules that might bind β-arrestins, then used additional tests to establish which candidates physically attached to the protein and stabilized it.

To see what that binding accomplished, the team tested promising compounds in engineered human cells that allowed GPCR signaling to be monitored as it happened. Experiments then moved into physiologically relevant immune cells and heart muscle cells, allowing the researchers to assess whether the effects held beyond simplified laboratory systems.

Three compounds emerged that prevented β-arrestins from being recruited to receptors. They blocked desensitization, which reduces a receptor’s responsiveness, and internalization, which moves receptors inside the cell. The compounds also suppressed β-arrestin-specific signaling. Tests across several GPCRs showed that G protein signaling remained intact, including at the GLP-1 receptor, where it continued longer than usual even during stimulation with Ozempic and Wegovy.

“We tested these compounds from every angle we could think of before we were convinced they were bona fide β-arrestin inhibitors,” Kahsai said.

Binding to a pocket reshapes β-arrestin

Pakharukova uncovered a structural explanation using cryo-electron microscopy. She visualized a compound called Cmpd-5 nestled in a previously unknown pocket on β-arrestin. Binding there altered the protein’s overall shape, leaving it unable to fully engage with GPCRs. This mechanism is called allosteric inhibition, because a molecule binding at one site changes how the protein functions elsewhere.

“Alem could have published a creditable paper about these molecules 10 years ago,” said Lefkowitz, Duke Health Distinguished Professor of Medicine and the study’s senior author. “But he’s a perfectionist. He wanted to figure out how they actually work.”

The ability to control β-arrestins with pharmacological precision could help researchers determine how individual signaling pathways influence metabolism, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and brain signaling. Eventually, adjusting those pathways could offer a route to more precise treatments with fewer unwanted side effects.

🚨 $INTC: Intel’s Comeback Is Getting Real — But Can It Actually Beat $NVDA, $AMD, and $TSM?

Revenue is accelerating. Server CPU demand is surging. Intel’s manufacturing ambitions are back in the spotlight. But one of the biggest questions in the semiconductor industry remains unanswered: Can Intel turn its comeback story into sustainable profits?

For years, Intel struggled with manufacturing delays, competitive pressure, and a costly restructuring. Meanwhile, rivals gained ground in high-performance computing, and AI transformed the semiconductor industry.

Now, the story is changing.

Intel’s second-quarter 2026 revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.1 billion. Its Data Center and AI business surged 59%, while adjusted earnings came in well above management’s previous guidance.

Those numbers suggest that Intel’s recovery may be gaining traction.

But there is a major difference between a company reporting a strong quarter and a company rebuilding a durable competitive advantage.

Intel still faces enormous manufacturing costs, fierce competition, and the challenge of convincing outside customers to trust its foundry business.

The bull case is that $INTC becomes a major beneficiary of the next AI infrastructure cycle. The bear case is that investors are pricing in a turnaround that the company has not yet fully delivered.

Here is what investors need to know before the next earnings report.

1. What Does Intel Actually Do?

Intel is one of the world's major semiconductor companies. Unlike companies that primarily design chips or manufacture them for others, Intel operates across several parts of the semiconductor value chain.

Its business has three major components.

Client computing: PCs and AI-enabled devices

Intel sells processors for laptops, desktops, and other client devices.

This business remains important because PCs continue to be a major source of revenue. AI-enabled PCs and newer processor generations could also support replacement demand as consumers and enterprises upgrade aging hardware.

However, Intel faces fierce competition from $AMD and from Arm-based designs, including processors used in systems built around technology from $ARM.

The opportunity is to defend its PC market position while improving performance, power efficiency, and product competitiveness.

The risk is that a weak PC replacement cycle or continued market-share losses could limit growth.

Data Center and AI: The server CPU opportunity

Intel's Data Center and AI segment sells processors and related products used in servers and data-center infrastructure.

This business is particularly important as AI workloads expand.

Although AI headlines often focus on GPUs, CPUs remain essential for general-purpose computing, orchestration, data processing, and many enterprise workloads.

Intel's newer Xeon processors could benefit if data-center customers increase CPU spending alongside their investments in AI accelerators.

The company's second-quarter results suggest that this opportunity is becoming more tangible.

Intel Foundry: The long-term strategic bet

Intel Foundry develops semiconductor manufacturing processes, produces chips for Intel's own product businesses, and aims to manufacture chips for outside customers.

This is the most ambitious part of Intel's turnaround.

The company wants to compete with established foundry leaders, particularly $TSM, by offering advanced manufacturing and packaging capabilities.

If Intel can attract major external customers and manufacture their chips at competitive yields, the foundry business could become a significant long-term growth engine.

But this is also where the execution risk is highest.

Building advanced manufacturing capacity requires enormous capital investment, technical expertise, and years of customer qualification. Winning a potential customer is not the same as securing a high-volume production contract.

Intel must prove that it can deliver competitive manufacturing technology, reliable yields, and attractive economics at scale.

2. The Numbers: Intel's Recovery Is Showing Real Momentum

Intel's second-quarter 2026 results provide the strongest evidence for the bullish argument.

Financial metricQ2 2026Q2 2025Revenue$16.1B$12.9BYear-over-year revenue growth+25%—GAAP gross margin40.4%27.5%Non-GAAP gross margin41.8%29.7%Non-GAAP EPS$0.42-$0.10Cash from operations$7.0B$2.1B

Source: Intel's official Q2 2026 earnings release.

Revenue growth of 25% is significant for a company of Intel's scale. Gross margin also improved sharply, suggesting better manufacturing execution, product mix, and operating performance.

The earnings result was especially notable: non-GAAP EPS of $0.42 compared with a loss of $0.10 a year earlier.

However, there is an important accounting detail.

Intel reported a GAAP net loss of approximately $11.0 billion, or $2.16 per share, in the same quarter. This was largely driven by a $12.529 billion mark-to-market loss associated with escrowed shares, rather than simply reflecting the performance of its core operating business.

That is why investors need to examine both GAAP and adjusted results.

The accounting adjustment does not erase the importance of the GAAP loss, but it helps explain why the reported net result differs so dramatically from the company's non-GAAP profit.

The more encouraging figure is that Intel generated $7.0 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter. However, its adjusted free cash flow remained deeply negative at approximately $8.4 billion, reflecting the substantial impact of partner contributions and other investment-related cash flows under the company's adjusted free cash flow calculation.

The takeaway is mixed:

Intel's operating performance is improving, but its capital-intensive business model remains a major challenge.

3. The Biggest Surprise: Data Center and AI Revenue Jumped 59%

Intel's Data Center and AI segment generated $6.3 billion in second-quarter revenue, up 59% year over year.

That is one of the most important figures in the company's recovery story.

The AI boom has created an enormous market for accelerators from $NVDA and other suppliers. But AI infrastructure also needs CPUs to coordinate workloads, support data processing, and run conventional enterprise applications.

Intel may be positioned to benefit if customers expand their CPU spending as their AI systems grow more complex.

The company has also introduced newer server products, including Xeon 6+ based on Intel 18A manufacturing technology.

If these products demonstrate competitive performance and customers continue increasing orders, Intel could strengthen its position in the data-center market.

But investors should avoid assuming that CPU growth automatically translates into a dominant position in AI computing.

Intel still competes with $AMD in server CPUs, while $NVDA has expanded its platform across GPUs, networking, and other data-center products.

The real question is whether Intel can sustain its growth rate after the recent rebound.

One strong quarter is encouraging. Several consecutive quarters of strong revenue, margins, and market-share performance would be much more convincing.

4. Intel 18A: The Technology That Could Change the Story

Intel's foundry strategy depends heavily on its ability to deliver advanced manufacturing technology.

Its Intel 18A process is designed to improve transistor performance and power efficiency. The company has also been advancing the related 18A-P process and developing the next-generation 14A node.

In its second-quarter announcement, Intel said a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 processors had entered high-volume manufacturing using Intel 18A and ASML's High-NA EUV technology.

That is a meaningful manufacturing milestone.

If Intel can achieve competitive yields, reliable production, and strong performance at scale, it could improve the competitiveness of its own products and strengthen its appeal to external foundry customers.

However, manufacturing leadership is not established by technology announcements alone.

Investors need to see evidence of:

Competitive process performance and power efficiency.

Improving manufacturing yields.

Reliable, high-volume production.

Customer commitments that translate into actual wafer demand.

A credible path toward sustainable foundry profitability.

Intel's own filings show why caution remains necessary.

In Q2 2026, Intel Foundry reported $5.765 billion in revenue, but its operating loss was $2.089 billion.

For the first half of 2026, foundry operating losses totaled $4.526 billion.

Importantly, much of this segment's revenue came from Intel's own internal manufacturing activity rather than outside customers. External foundry revenue was approximately $293 million in Q2, although that figure was affected by the transition of Altera to an external customer following a change in ownership.

This distinction is critical.

A foundry business that manufactures chips for its parent company is not the same as a foundry business that attracts large, profitable external customers.

Intel must demonstrate that outside customers are willing to commit meaningful production volumes and that those contracts can eventually support attractive returns on capital.

Source: Intel's Q2 2026 Form 10-Q.

5. The Bull Case: Four Reasons $INTC Could Have More Upside

Bullish factor No. 1: The business is recovering from a weak period

Intel's 25% year-over-year revenue growth and significant improvement in gross margin suggest that the business is performing better than it was a year earlier.

If that momentum continues, investors could begin to view Intel less as a struggling legacy chipmaker and more as a company with improving earnings power.

A sustained recovery could support higher earnings estimates and a reassessment of the stock's valuation.

However, the durability of that recovery matters more than the headline growth rate.

Bullish factor No. 2: Server CPU demand could remain resilient

AI infrastructure is expanding, and CPUs remain an important part of data-center architecture.

If demand for server CPUs remains strong, Intel could benefit from its existing customer relationships and its established position in enterprise computing.

The 59% growth in Data Center and AI revenue is an encouraging sign.

The next test is whether this growth persists as customers optimize their hardware spending and evaluate competing products from $AMD and other vendors.

Bullish factor No. 3: U.S. semiconductor manufacturing is strategically important

Intel operates leading-edge manufacturing and research facilities in the United States.

Domestic semiconductor manufacturing has become a strategic priority for policymakers and companies seeking more resilient supply chains.

That could help Intel attract customers that value geographic diversification, advanced packaging, and access to domestic manufacturing capacity.

But strategic importance is not a substitute for commercial competitiveness. Customers still need attractive pricing, reliable delivery, strong yields, and compelling technology.

Bullish factor No. 4: Intel could benefit from a successful foundry turnaround

If Intel 18A and future manufacturing nodes meet their technical and commercial goals, the company could gain new opportunities beyond its own processor business.

A successful foundry operation could provide another source of revenue and potentially improve the strategic value of Intel's manufacturing assets.

This is the largest potential long-term upside in the turnaround story.

It is also the outcome that requires the most execution.

Investors should distinguish between a promising manufacturing roadmap and evidence that external customers are committing to large-scale production.

6. The Bear Case: Five Risks That Could Derail Intel's Comeback

Risk No. 1: Foundry losses remain enormous

Intel Foundry's $2.089 billion operating loss in Q2 is a reminder of how expensive the turnaround remains.

The segment's revenue growth is encouraging, but its operating economics are not yet where investors would want them to be.

Advanced manufacturing requires continuous investment in equipment, research, facilities, and process development.

If utilization remains weak or yields fail to improve quickly enough, Intel could continue absorbing substantial losses.

The central question is not whether Intel can build advanced chips. It is whether it can manufacture them competitively and earn an acceptable return on the capital invested.

Risk No. 2: Competition from $TSM remains formidable

$TSM has a well-established foundry business and relationships with major semiconductor designers.

Intel needs to convince customers that its technology, capacity, packaging capabilities, and production execution are competitive alternatives.

That is a difficult task.

Even if Intel's process technology becomes attractive, customers may hesitate to move products away from established manufacturing partners because switching requires engineering work, qualification, and supply-chain planning.

Recent market reports have also highlighted competition in advanced packaging, where $TSM could offer alternatives if customers face capacity constraints at Intel.

That means Intel cannot rely solely on demand for advanced packaging. It must prove that customers will choose its solutions over alternatives.

Risk No. 3: Intel still faces serious competition in CPUs

The server and PC markets remain highly competitive.

$AMD continues to compete in CPUs, while Arm-based processors are expanding in some markets. In AI accelerators and broader data-center platforms, $NVDA has established a strong position.

Intel's recovery therefore depends on more than an overall expansion in semiconductor demand.

It needs to compete effectively on performance, power consumption, total cost of ownership, software support, and product availability.

If Intel grows revenue but loses market share in strategically important areas, the long-term investment thesis could weaken.

Risk No. 4: Capital spending could continue to pressure cash flow

Intel's manufacturing ambitions require substantial capital expenditure.

In Q2 2026, the company said it was meaningfully increasing investment in equipment, clean-room space, and substrates to support expected growth.

It also announced a €5 billion investment to expand manufacturing capacity for current and next-generation Xeon processors.

Such spending could create long-term value if demand and yields develop as expected.

But it also increases financial risk.

If customer demand falls short, factories are delayed, or manufacturing costs remain high, Intel could face prolonged pressure on free cash flow.

Investors should monitor not just revenue and adjusted earnings, but also capital expenditure, operating cash flow, free cash flow, and the company's overall funding requirements.

Risk No. 5: A strong quarter may already be reflected in the stock price

A recovering company can still be an unattractive investment if its share price assumes a nearly flawless turnaround.

Investors should compare Intel's valuation with its expected earnings, cash generation, capital requirements, and competitive position.

If the market already expects rapid margin recovery and significant external foundry wins, merely meeting those expectations may not be enough to drive additional gains.

The opposite is also true: if expectations are too pessimistic and Intel delivers sustained improvements, the stock could benefit.

Without a verified current share price and a detailed valuation model, it would be premature to label $INTC either cheap or expensive based on its operating recovery alone.

7. The Next Major Catalyst: Intel's Q3 Earnings on October 29

Intel is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results after the market closes on October 29.

Its previous guidance called for:

Q3 2026 metricManagement guidanceRevenue$15.8B–$16.8BGAAP gross marginApproximately 41.0%Non-GAAP gross marginApproximately 42.0%GAAP EPSApproximately $0.31Non-GAAP EPSApproximately $0.38

Source: Intel's official Q2 results and Q3 guidance.

These are management forecasts, not reported Q3 results.

For investors, the upcoming report will provide an important test of whether the recent improvement is sustainable.

Here are the key items to watch:

MetricWhat would strengthen the bull case?What would raise concerns?RevenueResults exceed guidance or outlook improvesRevenue misses or guidance weakensGross marginMargins improve alongside higher revenueCosts rise faster than salesServer CPUsContinued strong demand and shipmentsGrowth slows or competitive pressure increasesIntel 18AEvidence of reliable, scalable productionYield, timing, or customer-qualification problemsExternal foundryMore meaningful customer commitmentsAnnouncements fail to translate into production revenueCash flowBetter cash generation relative to investmentCapital spending continues to overwhelm operating cash flowFoundry lossesClear path toward improving economicsLosses remain elevated without credible improvement

A strong report could reinforce the view that Intel's recovery is gaining traction.

A weak report could revive concerns that the company is still struggling to turn technical progress and market demand into sustainable financial results.

8. The Bottom Line: A Real Turnaround Opportunity, but Not a Risk-Free Bet

Intel's investment story is more interesting today because the operating numbers are improving.

Revenue grew 25% year over year in Q2. Data Center and AI revenue climbed 59%. Non-GAAP EPS reached $0.42, and the company reported substantial improvements in gross margin.

These are meaningful developments.

But the risks remain equally important.

Intel Foundry continues to generate multibillion-dollar operating losses. External foundry revenue remains relatively small compared with the segment's overall revenue. Manufacturing expansion requires substantial investment, and competition from $TSM, $AMD, and $NVDA remains intense.

The optimistic scenario is that Intel combines stronger CPU demand with successful execution on Intel 18A and future manufacturing nodes, eventually turning its foundry business into a more competitive and profitable operation.

The pessimistic scenario is that product demand improves, but foundry economics, capital spending, and competition prevent the company from generating the returns investors expect.

My key takeaway: $INTC's recovery is becoming more credible, but the foundry turnaround still needs to be proven.

For investors, the most important evidence will not be another headline about AI demand or a new manufacturing milestone. It will be sustained revenue growth, improving margins, better cash generation, and real external customers committing to Intel's manufacturing technology.

October 29 could provide another important piece of that puzzle.

text:
On this day, Saturday, October 25, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Constitution ran Reuben R. Arnold's attack on the Frank jury at the top of Page 1, Column 1, under the headline "Jury Loaned Ears to Ravings of Mob, Says Rube Arnold." The story jumped to Page 14, Column 3. Arnold had started speaking at 4:13 on Friday afternoon, October 24, in the library of the State Capitol, where Judge L. S. Roan was hearing the defense motion for a new trial for Leo M. Frank.

Two months earlier, on August 25, 1913, a Fulton County jury had found Frank guilty of murdering 13 year old Mary Phagan at the National Pencil Company factory. A motion for a new trial asks the trial judge to set the verdict aside and start over. In Georgia the trial judge had to approve a verdict before it could stand, so Arnold aimed his whole speech at one man, Judge Roan.

Arnold told the judge that prejudice, not evidence, had convicted his client. He compared the case to the "ritual murder" trial of Mendel Beilis then going on in Kiev, Russia, and read aloud a letter from Emory College professor Julius McGath that the Constitution had printed the day before. He said the jurors sat "huddled together like a frightened herd of rabbits." He called Jim Conley, the factory sweeper whose testimony was the heart of the state's case, a "vile skunk" who repeated a memorized story like a parrot saying "Polly wants a cracker," and he said that without Conley there was no evidence at all. He told the court that if Frank hanged, Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey's conscience would drive him crazy. The library closed before he finished, so he picked up again Saturday morning.

The paper also covered the morning's work. The lawyers fought for three hours over the wording of the defense's 115 grounds before Judge Roan asked them to "cease scrapping." The court stenographers swore their record of the trial was correct. Then came the affidavits. Dorsey filed sworn statements from eight jurors, Higdon, Smith, Winburn, Townsend, Bosshart, Osborne, Jeffries and Metcalf, saying that A. H. Henslee, the juror the defense accused of being set against Frank before the trial, was the only man who opposed conviction on the first ballots. Other affidavits vouched for juror Marcellus Johenning and attacked the people who had sworn against both men. Every deputy and court officer on duty during the trial swore the jury never heard the crowd except for outbursts inside the courtroom, in front of the judge and both sets of lawyers, and the noise on the last day after the verdict was already in.

Arnold was one of the finest speakers in Georgia, and the prejudice he described was real in 1913. Ugly feeling against Jews existed, and he had every right to raise it. But a fear of prejudice is not proof that this jury acted on it, and the proof the court actually received pointed the other way. If Henslee had wanted Frank dead before he heard any testimony, it is hard to explain why his fellow jurors swore he was the last one to vote guilty, and only after an hour and several ballots. The defense's sidewalk witnesses said the jury must have heard the crowd. The deputies who were with the jury every day said, under oath, that it did not.

His attack on Conley left out what the jury actually weighed. The state never claimed Conley was an honest man. It argued that his story held up where other facts backed it. Monteen Stover, a state witness whom the defense now leaned on, found Frank's office empty between 12:05 and 12:10 that Saturday, the same stretch when Conley said Frank was in the back of the factory with Mary Phagan, while Frank told the jury he did not remember leaving his office. Conley also stood up to days of cross-examination by Luther Rosser, one of the hardest questioners in the state. Calling him a parrot did not explain why the defense could not break him. Judge Roan denied the new trial on October 31, 1913, and the Georgia Supreme Court upheld the verdict on February 17, 1914.

Appendix: Full article transcript

The Atlanta Constitution,

Saturday, 25th October 1913,

PAGE 1, COLUMN 1.

JURY LOANED EARS TO RAVINGS OF MOB, SAYS RUBE ARNOLD

Leo M. Frank Convicted, He Declares, by Prejudice and Not by the Evidence Given In Case.

HIS TRIAL IS COMPARED TO RITUAL MURDER CASE

Scratch Beneath the Surface and You Will Find Parallel With the Russian Trial, Arnold Tells Judge Roan.

Reuben Arnold, associate counsel for the defense, declared in his argument Friday for a new trial, that the trial of Leo Frank "would teach the entire universe a lesson against prejudice, and that civilization was horrified at the miserable example of his client's conviction."

His speech began at 4:13 o'clock. It was a vitriolic denunciation of the alleged reign of prejudice during Frank's arraignment, and of the fear the crowds inspired in the twelve men who meted the verdict of guilty to the prisoner. He compared the situation to the dark ages, when Jews were stoned to death because of their religion.

Prejudice was the theme of this argument. That and the dependence the jury and public put in the story of Jim Conley, the negro. The jury, he stated, did not listen to the evidence and weigh it as they should, but solely loaned their ears to the mad and ignorant ravings of the mob which "cried as wolves for the blood of the man on trial."

Taken Down in Shorthand.

His speech was delivered with all the fire and eloquence at the noted attorney's command. By special request of both the prosecution and defense, it was taken down by a stenographer, and will therefore go down into court history.

"A terrible responsibility is on the trial judge in this case, your honor," said Mr. Arnold. "The supreme court is the cause of this. It expects you to decide logically, to determine on the facts in the case whether or not a new trial should be granted. It is entirely up to you. In all supreme court cases, it is invariably said: 'These verdicts were either approved or renounced by the trial judge. We should act accordingly.'

"You must remember that the matter cannot be referred back to the jury. Those twelve men have been disbanded. They are of the past and cannot be brought back. I feel I am required by your honor's scope of power to argue these facts. We submit that the supreme court will not allow me to make argument, neither will anything else. Now is my only time. The supreme court, you know, is purely technical, that and nothing else.

"The Frank trial grew out of Georgia's most exceptional murder case. The killing of Mary Phagan was the most exceptional, the most diabolical. You will recollect that the most of our present-day murders are the slaying of women and children. This is a phenomenon with nothing for which to account. Twenty women, according to record, have been slain in Atlanta within the past two years.

Parallel With Russian Trial.

"In the trial of Frank, if you scratch beneath the surface, which we surely must do, you will find that the hue and cry is on an exact parallel with the Kiev trial in Russia, a Russian trial of a Jew for the murder of a thirteen-year-old girl. The Kiev trial has convinced the world that it is the most diabolic instance of persecution in civilized history; and the record of racial prejudice.

"We have had to contend with two hydra-headed propositions in the case of Frank. They are prejudice and ignorance. Also, might be added the spirit of the mob, the worst of all.

"The courts are supposed to be the superior knowledge in every case. They are supposed to be superior to the public and all else. But this case has made me tremble for the majesty and power of the court and for the reign of law and peacefulness. It seems as though the law, and power and justice is more on trial than Leo Frank.

"The ocean of feeling and prejudice that appeared at the trial threatened to wash justice away as though it were only a small and feeble building erected on the sands. I sincerely hope and pray I will never go through another such experience.

The Day is Coming.

"The day is now here when there should be no feeling against the Jew. It is coming with enlightenment and sincerity and knowledge. It is gaining ground with even such a thing as ignorance. In the south we have the best people, we have the representative aristocracy of our nation, and the southerner, brought down to a final analysis, is the only real American.

"But the ignorant southerner does not represent southern sentiment or feeling. And, it is only the ignorant who smile and shake hands with one another when a man is condemned to death, and a picture of a human being swung from the gibbet confronts a public. Listen! I have here something that bears as directly on the Frank case as any bit of evidence produced at the trial. It is a communication in The Constitution from a college professor of our own state. Let me read it:"

Letter to Constitution.

(Mr. Arnold then read a letter published in Friday's Constitution from Professor Julius McGrath, of the faculty of Emory college, Oxford, Ga. It follows:)

"Editor Constitution: In the holy city of Kiev, Russia, a Jew by the name of Mendel Bailiss is being tried on what is known as 'ritual murder', which, in plain English, means that this man had killed a Christian child in order to mix its blood with the Passover bread. In

Continued on Page Fourteen.

PAGE 14, COLUMN 3.

JURY LOANED EARS TO RAVINGS OF MOB

Continued From Page One.

the middle ages, which are appropriately called the dark ages, the then called Christians, with few exceptions, hated the Jews most unreasonably and ferociously. In order to injure and, if possible, to exterminate them, any means were considered justifiable, and hence the 'ritual murder' charge became a regular institution in many of the European countries.

"It was enough for anyone to say that he had seen a Jew murder a Christian child, when Jewish blood would flow like water in any European city. Some years ago an imperial investigation was undertaken in Russia, and it was unanimously reported that this charge against the Jews was without the slightest foundation in fact, and that as a nation the Jews abhorred the shedding of blood, and that a Jewish murderer was the rarest exception. In spite of it, these false accusations are used from time to time, and the 'pogroms,' which are nothing more than mob murders of the Jews, are usually started in ritual murder accusations, the ignorant Russian priests frequently inciting the ignorant populace.

"A resolution adopted on the 15th instant by the house of deputies of the Episcopal church, consisting of lay and clerical delegates, now in triennial session in the city of New York, condemned the attitude of Russia in charging the Jews with such groundless crime, and called upon the church there to stop its persecution of the Jews. I am very friendly to the Episcopal church, the greatest Christian mission to the Jews is carried on by that church in England, and its efforts have been crowned with marvelous success. Among the Christian Jews the direct result of the great mission of that church are men of great distinction who have done honor to the church and to the countries in which they have lived. Yet truth compels me to say that if the Episcopal church did not directly encourage it, it at least unconsciously, perhaps, has given excuse to the ignorant in their prejudice toward the Jews. In the collect for Good Friday in every Episcopal church in the land the Jews are classed with the infidels, Turks and heretics, and prayer is offered for the conversion of that motley crowd, the Jews being among them. No intelligent Jew takes the matter seriously; neither does any intelligent Christian. On the other hand, where there are some on both sides that are not intelligent, it certainly cannot advance cordial feelings between them. It is true that this general convention proposes to amend the prayer so it shall read 'for ancient Jews' instead of 'for all Jews,' but I do not see how this change will help. A gentleman said to me the other day: 'Ever since the Jews crucified Christ, it is difficult to get justice for the Jew.' He may have overstated the matter, but it is true that the ignorant prejudice from which the Jew suffers is due not to the fact that he himself is unworthy, but largely to the other fact that nearly twenty centuries ago some Jews had a hand in Christ's death.

"I am glad that in this blessed America these prejudices are gradually dying out, and I am looking to this country to teach all countries that it is criminal to harbor prejudice, and that the twentieth century is not called upon nor will it undertake to carry out a program that was prepared in the days of the inquisition. It were better not to pray at all than to mix narrow-mindedness, ignorance and utterances that were dictated by an age that has been repudiated by all who love God and humanity.

"JULIUS M'GATH.

"Oxford, Ga."

Relentless Effort to Convict.

"And this communication from Professor McGath accounts better than anything for the relentless effort made to convict Leo Frank.

"Was it ever before brought to your minds that the only conclusive witness against the man was an accessory to the crime, and was the lowest, most debased criminal in Atlanta's court record? Also the only man who testified to perversion?

"Time, however, rights everything. It is the world's greatest teller of truth. In the end, time and truth prevail. It takes time for truth, and truth forever follows time. Time rectifies all and everything, and everybody.

"Men grow weak in time of excitement. Impulsiveness causes all of us to lose a certain amount of strength. We became absurd, cowardly, ridiculous. Such was the condition in the trial of Frank. His conviction was a case of fanaticism that would have excelled the assassination of Abraham Lincoln. It was all due to temper and excitement and prejudice.

"Everything was lost on the jury, facts, argument, logic, soundness and sense. It was like casting pearls before swine. They were huddled together like a frightened herd of rabbits, afraid to move, afraid to do right, afraid to administer justice.

How Horrible is Prejudice.

"This case will do more than anything to show the entire world just how horrible is race prejudice. It will have a national bearing, and will convince the world of the ignorance and savagery of prejudicial feeling. The whole universe will learn a lesson. God meant it so. We are now molding a universal feeling, righting a universal wrong.

"The jury believed this criminal negro before they would believe the intellectual Frank, logic, wisdom and the most powerful alibi ever presented. It was outrageous. It not only reflects on the intellect of the jury, but upon the people of our southland.

"Outside of Conley there is no evidence whatever on which to convict. If the negro's vile story had not played its part in the trial, I do not doubt that your honor would have discharged the jury and stopped the trial for lack of evidence. Take an ordinary case, for instance. Would you have hesitated an instant? No! Certainly not. You nor any other justice.

"Why, the inflammatory speech of Hugh Dorsey would have killed the case. Have we taken leave of our senses? Have we broken all rules of civilization, all rules of God our Maker and Keeper? Frank is doomed to death, doomed on evidence that would not have convicted a Jew of the darkest ages, when men were stoned and hanged by their toes to die.

"It is peculiar, but true, also sad, that modern people love to believe black and dirty things. It is an inheritance, it seems, that comes with the furious trend of modern life. They did it in this case, believed the blackest, filthiest lies ever told. There doesn't live a wolf, or bear, or snake, so utterly devoid of conscience and knowledge of right and justice as this monstrous negro Conley, and yet, the men put absolute faith and credence in his stinking lie.

Will You Believe Vile Tale?

"Are you going to believe the tale of this vile skunk? Are you? It's up to you, finally. From the very beginning, the whole situation was strained. People were willing to grasp at anything, to strain at anything. Everywhere you could hear: 'Sure, that damned Jew did it. Why go further for the murderer?'

"Nobody wanted to believe that anybody but the 'Damned Jew' did it. Everybody wanted to believe that he did it. And this sentiment aptly showed the fact that the hardest thing to do on earth is to argue against prejudice. It is hardest for these reasons: First, because fairmindedness is required; second, because courage is required.

"You may find one of these traits in a man, but it is seldom you find both. The jury might have had one or the other, but I doubt it had both. And, both are required to fight such a venomous evil as prejudice.

"When all this persecution centered on Frank, every conceivable kind of lie sprang up against him. And, the truth of the matter was that most of them came from volunteers. The sea of prejudice threatened to wash him completely into oblivion. And, Conley's lies composed more than half of that sea that finally did the washing. Wasn't it shameful?

"Yet, some poor, deluded souls say: 'Why didn't you break him down. He was telling the truth, or you'd have broken him.' God help such people. Why, after this negro had been on the stand for two days or longer, he never mentioned the whereabouts of the dead girl's purse until prompted by Dorsey.

"They say he stayed on the stand and withstood every attack. Certainly he did. So would have a parrot. You can take one of those birds and teach it to say, 'I want a cracker,' and you can't break it. It's impossible. You have to knock him down. The jury was hoodwinked, that's all.

Plastered Over With Lies.

"Conley was so plastered over with lies and contradictions that it was monstrous to put faith in one iota of what he said. He had his little wretched tale all canned and stocked in his system, and he poured it out to the jury as though megaphoning it. He might have said: 'Polly wants a cracker,' just as a bird that is taught such sayings will echo whenever prompted.

"He is willing to believe and assert anything that will save his neck from the gibbet of popular opinion.

"Lanford and his cohorts wouldn't allow Jim Conley to confess. Every time the negro bordered on a confession of guilt the detectives shifted him off to accusations of Frank.

"The whole trial has never been equaled in the world of justice. It was nothing but an effort to try Frank by prejudice for every conceivable crime in the catalogue of misdeeds. It was the unfairest on record, the most miserable. Why, one instance to prove it is the injection by Dorsey of the perversion evidence, which was done merely to prejudice the jury and inflame the men who already were frightened to their wit's end.

"If Leo Frank is hanged, I'd rather be dead and rotting in my grave than in Hugh Dorsey's place. His conscience will drive him crazy, distracted, and to God only knows what end. And it will be no less than his deserts. There never was a charge against Frank until the trial, never a blemish. And they grew from the mire and filth with prejudice as their roots."

At this point, the keeper of the library, in which the hearing was being held, notified the judge that it was closing time. Mr. Arnold's speech was discontinued until this morning at 9 o'clock.

Friday Morning Session.

For three hours Friday morning the monotonous disputes between Dorsey and Rosser and Arnold over the 115 counts, based on allegation of fact, were made continuous. When the noon hour was reached the end of the motion certification was completed so far as either side would concede at that time, and the court then stood ready to proceed with other matters in the case. The conclusion of the motion marked the end of a two-day dispute between the attorneys engaged on both sides of the case, which, since its inception, had proven acrimonious and even ill-tempered at times.

When Friday's session opened Judge Roan, who had been unusually patient with both sides, urged the attorneys for more haste in their work. His request met with instant favor, and the session was marked by less friction and more accomplished results than were the sessions of Wednesday and Thursday.

"I wish you gentlemen would cease scrapping," admonished the court, with a smile, when the session opened. "These little points are not worth all this argument," Judge Roan added.

Still fighting each step stubbornly, the attorneys followed the court's wishes, and by noon the defense had cleared away all of its affidavits charging bias against certain jurors who had been on the Frank jury.

During the morning session Dorsey and Arnold disputed for the better part of an hour over the testimony of Detective Black. One ground of the motion recited that Black testified that Frank had employed counsel when he arrived at police barracks the Monday morning after the murder. Dorsey disputed this flatly and the record was consulted, with the result that the wording of the motion was changed to allege that Black testified Frank "had counsel" at that time instead of "had employed counsel."

Points Cleared Up.

Several points that were left in dispute Thursday were quickly cleared up when Attorney Arnold was sworn and stated that to the best of his belief that the allegations of fact contained in the defense motion were true and in the defense motion that when the record did not bear out the filed motion he would consent to Attorney Arnold being sworn and testifying about these points.

The court stenographers who made shorthand notes of the Frank trial were sworn during the morning session and declared that they had taken a correct record of the entire case. This was done on account of the fact that the defense declared that several objections that had made on certain motions were not recorded in the transcript of the case.

At noon the discussion of the motion was ended and the defense at once began the reading of its affidavits.

Jurors Defend Henslee.

A number of Frank jurors came to the defense of their accused fellow-juryman, A. H. Henslee, during the hearing Friday, when affidavits from them were submitted by Solicitor Dorsey, attesting to Henslee's attitude toward the prisoner when the first ballots were cast for a verdict.

Henslee was the only juror to oppose conviction, the jurors swore. With tears in his eyes, he is said to have told the eleven other men that a man's life was not to be handled carelessly, and that it should be weighed and sifted before sending a human to the gallows.

It required several votes and an hour or so to bring Henslee to his verdict of guilty, it was attested. Each of the jurors testified to his good character and to their readiness to personally appear in his behalf. There were also a number of affidavits from prominent men, both in Atlanta and other Georgia cities who spoke highly of the accused man's character.

The character of Marcellus Johenning, another juror under fire, was also upheld by a large number of affidavits from business men all over the state. On the other hand, the solicitor produced affidavits attacking the character and veracity of a number of affiants whose affidavits assailing Henslee and Johenning were produced by the defense.

Letters Attack Frank.

Colonel Arnold created surprise at the afternoon session when he declared to Judge Roan that one of his best proofs of extreme racial prejudice that was prevalent during the trial was the mass of letters he had received from anonymous persons, all of which were threatening.

"And not one of them," he declared, "failed to contain the expression: 'That damned Jew!'"

Affidavits from every deputy and court attache engaged at the court house during the trial were introduced by the solicitor. Each attested to the fact that during no time did the jury hear the demonstrations from the crowd, excepting when they occurred in the courtroom before the gaze and hearing of the judge and attorneys for both sides, and on the day of the verdict after the decision had been rendered.

Among those who swore to this were Plennie Miner, R. B. Deavors, J. C. Lewis, clerk of court; Drew Liddell and other court deputies. The jurors who swore to affidavits defending Henslee and Johenning were Jurors Higdon, Smith, Winburn, Townsend, Bosshart, Osborne, Jeffries, and Metcalf.

[A professional card for Solicitor Dorsey's law firm, printed on Page 11, Column 7, and linked to this article on https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI, is omitted here.]

Source: The Atlanta Constitution, Oct. 25, 1913, via https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI

text:
How the Iranian Battlespace Has Changed - David Ignatius (Washington Post)
The chapter of the U.S.-Iran conflict that began in February changed the Middle East battlespace, likely forever. Deterrence failed. U.S. military bases in the region were ravaged. Rather than preventing Iranian attacks, Centcom's forward bases turned out to be a magnet for them.
The old regime in Tehran was decapitated, but it was replaced by cocky hard-liners who seem convinced they can outlast a war-weary superpower.
U.S. forces are surging into the region, and commanders are said to be preparing military options for President Donald Trump. One ominous sign is that the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh ordered some employees to leave, and other U.S. embassies in the region are reportedly making similar moves.
Trump sent Vice President JD Vance to Islamabad to offer what the administration called a "golden bridge" to the future for Iran if it would meet U.S. demands. What emerged was the wobbly MOU, which quickly collapsed.
After that failure, Trump combined armed escorts of Western oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz with economic strangulation of Iran. That combination, to me, has been the president's most successful approach to date. But it hasn't guaranteed his red line: Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.
U.S. Central Command, which has been preparing to fight Iran for a generation, was rocked by Tehran's use of drones and missiles. The Fifth Fleet's headquarters in Bahrain was severely damaged, and the Navy won't return there "anytime soon," according to Adm. Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations.
Centcom's huge air base at Al Udeid in Qatar was also battered, though air operations for the region had been relocated mostly to South Carolina beforehand. For now, Centcom will have to rely on stand-off forces at sea and distant air bases.  https://t.co/RCOXY08svV

The Trump administration suspended sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and reached an agreement with Moscow on supplies—a move that, according to The New York Times, dealt a serious blow to Ukraine and its European allies.

The newspaper reports that the announcement caught Ukrainian and European officials off guard as they were holding meetings with American envoys in Miami. Kiev called the decision “weak” and “unworthy of partners,” while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting the sanctions would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue the war.

Moreover, according to the NYT, Trump simultaneously increased pressure on Kiev, demanding that it stop strikes on Russian oil refineries and publicly calling on Ukraine to “get a new president.”

In exchange for US concessions, Putin offered nothing beyond continuing the war, the newspaper observes. Just minutes after the deal was announced, the Kremlin confirmed that it had no intention of resuming negotiations.

The publication emphasizes that the White House’s motivation is tied to domestic politics: Trump wants to bring fuel prices down ahead of the midterm elections. To achieve this, he is prepared to pressure Kiev into bargaining away its leverage without any reciprocal commitments from Moscow.

The article also cites the assessment that the deal “effectively puts Washington on the same side as Moscow against Ukraine.”

text:
On a crisp autumn day, October 25,1764, John Adams and Abigail Smith were married in the parlor of her family’s home in Weymouth, Massachusetts. Abigail’s father, a Congregational minister, performed the ceremony for the young couple. John, then a rising lawyer from nearby Braintree, and Abigail, the daughter of a well-regarded local family, had known each other for several years. 

Their early meetings had been casual, but a growing affection developed through letters exchanged during periods of separation caused by John’s work and a bout of illness. After the simple service, the newlyweds rode together to the modest farmhouse John had inherited, beginning a life that would soon be shaped by the gathering tensions between the colonies and Britain.

Their union joined two people of different social standing yet similar intellectual energy. John brought a Harvard education, a budding legal career, and a practical disposition shaped by rural New England life. Abigail brought a sharp mind honed by reading and conversation, along with the confidence of a household accustomed to learning and public service. From the start she showed a readiness to manage domestic affairs, a skill that would prove essential as John’s professional duties often kept him away. Within a year their first child arrived, and the young family settled into a rhythm of farm life, household management, and the ordinary challenges of raising children in colonial Massachusetts.

Over more than five decades the marriage endured long absences, political upheaval, and the demands of public life. Abigail’s letters offered John both personal support and clear-eyed advice during the years leading to independence and the early republic, while she kept their home and finances in order. Their correspondence later revealed a partnership grounded in mutual respect and shared purpose. The couple raised a family that included a future president, and their private bond became one of the best-documented relationships of the founding era, illustrating how personal commitment could sustain public service through war, diplomacy, and the creation of a new nation.

🇷🇺🇮🇳⚡ According to reports, Russia has offered India its most advanced air and missile defense system, the S-500, but with additional conditions attached to the proposed purchase agreement, which could complicate India’s already ambitious plans to modernize its armed forces. Russia wants a minimum order of five S-500 regiments.

India, which is seeking to eliminate critical gaps in its air defense system, is considering acquiring five more S-400 systems, almost a decade after signing the initial agreement with Moscow. Despite the long wait, Russia has still not completed deliveries under the original contract, and the fifth S-400 system remains undelivered.

Meanwhile, India’s Ministry of Defence is also considering the acquisition of one or two S-500 systems to strengthen its strategic defenses, in particular through advanced missile defense and anti-satellite weapons.

However, the new conditions put forward by the Kremlin threaten to increase pressure on India’s already overstretched defense budget.

At the same time, New Delhi is pursuing several major procurement programs, including:

⬛ 114 Rafale fighter jets, as well as Rafale-M aircraft for Indian Navy aircraft carriers.

⬛ Submarines with air‑independent propulsion (AIP) to strengthen its undersea warfare capabilities.

⬛ Large-scale replenishment of missile and ammunition stocks, after significant losses in the May conflict with Pakistan, when Pakistani strikes destroyed substantial amounts of military supplies at Indian ammunition depots, including the depot in Beas.

With several costly defense procurements competing for limited financial resources, the conditions set by Moscow for the S-500 deal may force New Delhi to make difficult procurement decisions, potentially delaying plans to build a more comprehensive, multilayered air and missile defense system.

This situation also underscores India’s continued dependence on Russian defense technologies, despite delivery delays, rising procurement costs, and competing military priorities that complicate its long-term modernization ambitions.

text:
A dead family dog was turned away from a cemetery outside Washington because the ground was divided into a white section and a Black section. The man driving the car was Ralph Bunche, who within a decade brokered the 1949 armistice agreements between Israel and four Arab states and became the first person of African descent to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

When Harry Truman offered him what the Black press of the day called the highest federal post ever opened to a Black American, he turned it down and told the President's own envoy that the cemetery was the reason. His young daughters had only wanted the dog buried properly, so ask yourself how many grown men had to sign off before that line got drawn through a pet cemetery.

On an afternoon in the early 1940s a man drove out of Washington with a dead dog in his car.

The dog belonged to his daughters. Joan and Jane were small girls then, and they were the ones who had asked that it be done properly.

That is what he was doing out there. Buying a plot for an animal, the way people did.

There was an office. There was a man behind a desk who did this for a living, and who had a price and a procedure and no reason to expect trouble.

The man behind the desk explained that the cemetery had two sections.

One piece of ground was for the pets of white families. The other piece of ground, set apart, was for the pets of Black families.

Take a second with that, because the paperwork is the part that gets you.

Somebody had walked that field. Somebody had decided where the line ran and put a stake in it, and somebody had written it down and priced it and trained the staff to say it out loud to a customer without dropping his eyes.

None of that happens by accident. It happens because a group of grown men sat in a room and worked out how to keep dead dogs segregated by the color of the people who had fed them.

The father in the car was not a nobody who could be dismissed. He held a doctorate from Harvard, ran a department at Howard University, and was at that moment working inside American military intelligence on the war.

Within a decade he would negotiate the armistice agreements that ended the 1948 war in the Middle East, and win the Nobel Peace Prize.

His name was Ralph Bunche, and he was told to take the dog around to the other section.

He drove home to his daughters and they buried the dog, and he did not forget a single detail of it. Six or seven years later, the President of the United States offered him the highest position ever offered to a Black American.

That afternoon at the cemetery is the reason he said no.

Bunche had every reason to believe Washington could be lived in, because he had already bet his savings on it. In 1941 he hired Hilyard Robinson, one of the finest Black architects in the country, and had him build a modern house at 1510 Jackson Street Northeast in the Brookland neighborhood.

Not a rental, not a stop along the way. A house he commissioned and put his family into.

His wife Ruth had been one of his students at Howard, the youngest of ten children out of Montgomery, Alabama, and she taught in the District's public schools.

He had not come from anything. Both his parents were dead before he was fourteen, and his grandmother Lucy Taylor Johnson took him and his sisters into her house in Los Angeles and pushed him through school.

He was valedictorian at Jefferson High. He finished at the top of his class at UCLA in 1927, and in 1934 he became the first African American in the country to earn a doctorate in political science.

He built the house because he thought the city was worth building a house in. Washington spent the next several years correcting him.

There is one scene from those years that explains the argument Bunche was having with his whole profession, and it happened at a jail somewhere in the American South at the end of the 1930s.

Two men were doing field research for what would become the most famous book ever written about American race relations. One was Gunnar Myrdal, a Swedish economist the Carnegie Corporation had hired to run the study.

The other was Bunche, who before the project ended would hand Myrdal more than three thousand pages of his own research.

At midday the warden offered lunch. He seated Myrdal at his own table.

Bunche was sent out to eat with the Black chain gang.

Afterward the two of them argued about it, and the argument was the whole future of the country in miniature.

Myrdal thought the warden had to have felt something. A man does not split a lunch in two like that without knowing what he is doing, and Myrdal believed that knowledge would work on the warden's conscience, and on America's, until the country fixed itself.

Bunche said the warden felt nothing at all.

That was the disagreement. One of them was making a prediction about white America, and the other one was going to spend the rest of his life being the test case.

In 1942 a young Army captain named Dean Rusk, who worked alongside Bunche on Asia intelligence, asked him to lunch and walked him into the officers' dining room at the War Department. It was a cafeteria that seated four or five hundred men.

Rusk said later that he simply had not known Black men did not eat in that room. He found out.

Nothing was said to their faces. The complaints came afterward, moving up the chain of command, and they were not even aimed at Bunche.

They were aimed at Rusk, phrased as a question about what Rusk thought he was doing bringing him in there.

Rusk's colonel backed him and nothing came of it. Rusk carried the memory for the next forty years.

What nobody wrote down was the other half of it. Nobody recorded what that walk to the table was like for the only Black man in a room of four hundred officers, or what he did with his face while he ate.

That side of the day was not considered worth a note.

In 1946 he left Washington for the United Nations. Two years later he was made chief aide to Count Folke Bernadotte, the Swedish diplomat sent to mediate the war in Palestine.

On 17 September 1948 Bernadotte was assassinated.

The entire thing landed on Bunche. He was named acting mediator, and he took it to the island of Rhodes and did not come off it for the better part of a year.

The delegations would not sit in the same room. In some cases they would not formally acknowledge that the other side existed.

So he put them in separate rooms and walked between them himself. He carried each position down the corridor, took the answer, walked back, and started again.

When a delegation stormed out he waited for them to come back and began again from where they had stopped.

Between February and July of 1949 he got signatures on four armistice agreements, between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. The lines he drew held for close to twenty years.

He had just proved, on a world stage, that he could get men to share a table who had every reason on earth not to.

In April 1949 Harry Truman offered him the post of Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern and African Affairs. It would have made him the highest ranking Black official in the history of the United States government, with a clear road toward running the department one day.

Bunche said no.

Truman did not accept that and sent someone to change his mind. He sent Dean Rusk, the same man from the War Department cafeteria, by then a senior State Department official and later Secretary of State under Kennedy.

Rusk came up to New York. It came around to lunchtime and he asked Bunche to eat with him, and over that meal he made the President's case.

Bunche told him he appreciated it and could not do it. He said that as a father he was not able to ask his children to live the way they would have to live in Washington.

Then he told Rusk about the dog.

He described driving out to the pet cemetery and being turned away, and he delivered the ending of it as a dry joke, with a laugh, the way a man does when the alternative is something else. The punchline was that "the dog was black."

Rusk took that back to the President of the United States. Truman was sorry about it and let it go.

Then Bunche said it to Truman's face. He called at the White House in late May 1949 and told the President directly that he had decided to decline, and the wire report carrying the news on 26 May noted that he spent the rest of the meeting briefing Truman on the stalled Syrian armistice talks.

He turned down the job and went straight back to doing the country's work anyway. The man who took the post instead, George McGhee, was named almost immediately.

Bunche then did something he almost never did, which was to say it in public. He told a reporter that Jim Crow in Washington was no secret, that "no Negro finds Jim Crow congenial," and that he was a Negro.

On a Fourth of July broadcast he put it harder, describing life in the nation's capital, for any Black person who hated segregation, as something you served out like a sentence.

The country had made him the biggest offer it had ever made to a Black man. He answered it with a plot of dirt for a dog.

On 18 October 1949 New York City gave Ralph Bunche a ticker tape parade up lower Broadway. Nehru had gone up the same route the day before.

There is a granite strip in the sidewalk down there with his name on it and the words United Nations mediator. The following year he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, the first person of African descent ever to receive it.

Six months before that parade he had told the President he could not raise his children in the capital of his own country. Both things are true, and they happened in the same year, to the same man.

Four years after the Nobel, his own government asked him to prove he was not a traitor.

On 27 and 28 May 1954 the newspapers carried the news that the Nobel Peace Prize winner was being put through a loyalty investigation by the board set up to examine Americans working for international organizations.

The hearing was closed. The evidence has stayed secret.

What the New York Times and others did print was the names of the two men accusing him. One of them was Manning Johnson.

Johnson was a professional informer on the Justice Department payroll, a former Communist official who had turned testifying into a career. That same year a University of Washington professor named Melvin Rader published a piece in The New Republic titled The Profession of Perjury, laying out how Johnson's sworn testimony against him had been false.

That was the caliber of witness the United States government put in front of Ralph Bunche. The charge was that he had attended a Communist Party meeting in May 1935.

He answered it with a document running over a hundred pages. He sat down and defended his life on paper, line by line, at the age of fifty, four years after Oslo.

While that was going on, the CIA was asking him for advice and the White House was trying to send him to Europe on a goodwill tour to represent the United States.

There is one more thing in the file. In 1941, the same year he was building the house on Jackson Street, the FBI had designated Ralph Bunche for custodial detention in the event of a national emergency.

They had him on a list of people to be picked up and held.

He was cleared in 1954. No apology is recorded.

Then came the summer of 1959, and this time it was his son's turn.

Ralph Junior, the youngest child and still in his teens, was taking tennis lessons at the West Side Tennis Club in Forest Hills, Queens. The club professional was a man named George Agutter.

Agutter liked the boy. He was good enough that the pro suggested he go ahead and apply for a junior membership, which is the ordinary thing that happens to a teenager who can play.

The application went up. It came back down.

The club president, Wilfred Burglund, told Bunche that the club did not accept Jews or Negroes, and explained the reasoning as though it were obvious. A private club, he said, is like a private house, where you get to "invite whom you want to."

Understand where his father was standing at that moment. Ralph Bunche was Under Secretary of the United Nations, nine years a Nobel laureate, a man whose signature had ended a war.

His boy still could not get on the court.

It hit the papers and the club panicked. It apologized, the man who had said the quiet part out loud was gone within weeks, and it offered Bunche himself a membership.

He turned that down too, and his reason was exact. The offer had been made because of who he was, and the rule underneath it had not moved an inch for anybody else's son.

The Atlanta Daily World reported that July what he did with the money instead. He bought a five hundred dollar membership in the NAACP.

He never stopped showing up in person. He walked his first picket line in 1937 and organized his Howard students onto picket lines against segregated stores and theaters in Washington, and he sat on the NAACP board for more than twenty years.

In March 1965, with diabetes already breaking him down, he flew to Alabama and walked in the front rank out of Selma alongside Martin Luther King Junior, Ralph Abernathy and Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel. He spoke at the capitol in Montgomery on the twenty-fifth.

The young men coming up behind him were not impressed. Stokely Carmichael's line about him was "You can't have Bunche for lunch."

It was meant as an insult about a man who solved other people's problems overseas. It was also, without anyone intending it, an accurate description of a life that had been decided at meals.

The warden's table. The officers' cafeteria in the War Department.

The rooms on Rhodes he walked between for eleven months, and the lunch in New York where he told Dean Rusk no.

Which brings it back to that jail in the South, and the question the two of them argued about. Myrdal had bet that white America's conscience would eventually do the work.

Bunche had said the warden felt nothing at all.

Bunche was the one who got to find out. He tested it with the biggest job his country had ever put in front of a Black man, and the answer came back as a segregated burial ground for animals.

The United States would not have a Black Secretary of State until 2001. That is fifty-two years after Ralph Bunche was offered the road that led there and would not take it.

The house is still standing at 1510 Jackson Street Northeast, in Brookland. It went onto the National Register of Historic Places in 1993, twenty-two years after he died, and in 2001 the D.C. Preservation League listed it as an endangered place.

It is the house he built when he still thought the bet was worth making. He never moved his family back into it.

His terms were never complicated and he never raised them. His children were to be able to live in the capital city of their own country the way anybody else's children lived in it.

He died in 1971 without ever being handed it.

So the next time you pass a cemetery, think about how much ground one man had to move to get a single plot of it, and how he drew four national borders and never got that one.

if your close rate is high but you're exhausted, you don't have a sales problem — you have a qualification problem.

closing everyone feels like talent. in an alabama service shop it often means the filter is missing and every "win" is eating nights. i score wins on energy now, not just GHL deposits.
