(P.S. why this matters is at the bottom)

1/ look at win quality, not just win rate
in GHL, tag your last 10 wins: margin okay? · change-order count · paid on time? · energy drain 1–5.
high close + low joy = wrong ICP slipping through GHL calendar.

2/ tighten intake before the call
required buckets: budget · timeline · decision-maker · what does success look like in 90 days?
chaos answers → async written/video intake only, or a polite no. your calendar is inventory.

3/ raise price or raise the floor
run +15–25% on the next 5 quotes OR enforce a walk-away number written in GHL.
some wins should become graceful nos with a referral to a cheaper fit.

4/ publish exclusions on GHL offer page
not-a-fit lines fire bad clients before you shake hands.
if they argue with the list on call 1, believe them.

5/ sales script add-on
ask: what would make this a bad hire for you?
serious buyers answer. tourists shrug. shrug → soft exit, keep the door warm.

6/ capacity reset week
if you're underwater: pause new sales 7–14 days, clear delivery debt, reopen with tighter filters and a later start date (sold as a feature with GHL deposit to hold the slot).

why this matters:

text:
What kind of man could become one of the most famous figures in the history of America’s Appalachian mountains? William Anderson “Devil Anse” Hatfield, born in 1839, was a determined and formidable figure whose name would eventually become inseparable from one of the most legendary family feuds in American history. In this historic photograph, Hatfield sits proudly on horseback, carrying a rifle and wearing a cartridge belt, presenting the rugged image of a man shaped by the hardships and traditions of the nineteenth-century frontier.

Hatfield was the patriarch of the Hatfield family, which became locked in a bitter and prolonged rivalry with the McCoy family along the border of West Virginia and Kentucky. What began as a series of personal disagreements, disputes over property, and tensions between families gradually grew into a conflict that captured public attention across the country. With strong family loyalties and a reputation for determination, Devil Anse became a central figure in the feud, a story that would later inspire books, documentaries, television productions, and countless retellings of the Old West and Appalachian past.

Yet behind the famous nickname and the stories of family rivalry was a real man who lived through a changing America, witnessing decades of hardship, conflict, and transformation before his death in 1921. Today, photographs like this offer a glimpse into a world when reputation, family loyalty, and local disputes could shape a person’s place in history for generations. When you look at this image of Devil Anse Hatfield mounted on horseback, do you see a symbol of frontier toughness, or a reminder of how deeply family rivalries can shape the course of history?

text:
I said yes to cold email before I knew how to run it.

Now I'm Head of GTM at Pipeline Tech, and our team has sent 10M+ cold emails for 100+ B2B companies.

I'm 24 and came from a short-form content agency (not a technical guy at all), and looking back, one thing decided all of it.

RESULTS ON DEMAND.

Running outbound for a client means a lot has to go right at once:

> Who you target
> An offer worth replying to
> Inboxes that land
> Copy
> Replies inside 5 minutes
> Reporting the client trusts
> Booking the meeting

Producing results whenever a client needs them is what keeps them around.

3 moves I made to get there:

1) I turned my content agency into a cold email agency, because a lot of my clients weren't big personalities and content needed them to be

2) I told the first client who asked "I'll learn how to do it and I'll run it for you", then learned it through a couple of courses and a lot of trial and error

3) I built my own dashboards (every client against our agency averages) and I check them every morning

Once results stopped depending on how a client came across on camera, I could convert clients much faster.

If your clients' results depend on their personality, add a channel that doesn't.

I have seen that this fact is true for both B2B & consumer apps. New features, issues, independent or driven by change in the course of the external world (trends, new tech, cybersecurity incidents etc).

Other than that, you need constant touch points with your users.

Software buyers need to be explained that this is a life-long commitment, just like a car has life-long upkeep & maintenance. This pain is worth it because of the value it offers vs. the alternatives.

For this reason, you cannot or should not have one-man dependent software. This key man risk is real and boutique consultants should work around this, lessen it as much as possible. Small team 2-3 guys is fine. Just not one person.

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

text:
In 1967 a young man stopped for a hurt old man lying by a Nevada highway. Nine years later he was named in a will worth $156 million.

He was 23, driving alone at night on a desert highway north of Las Vegas. He saw an old man lying in the dirt by the road.

The man was thin, dirty and hurt. The young man took him for a drifter or an old prospector. He offered to take him to a hospital. The old man refused. He just wanted a ride to Las Vegas.

So he drove him there and dropped him off behind the Sands Hotel. Along the way the old man told him who he was. The young man did not believe him.

In April 1976 the old man died. He was one of the richest men in America, and nobody could find his will. People punched holes in walls looking for it.

Three weeks later an envelope turned up at church headquarters in Salt Lake City. Inside was a handwritten will. One line left a sixteenth of the estate, about $156 million, to a name nobody recognized.

The young man from the desert. By then he ran a small gas station in Utah.

At first he said he knew nothing about it. Then his fingerprint was found on the envelope. He admitted he had delivered it and said a stranger had left it at his gas station.

In 1978 a jury decided the will was a forgery. He never got a penny.

He never changed his story. Decades later a retired FBI agent said a pilot claimed he had flown the old man to a brothel near that same highway that very night. Others call it nonsense.

Hollywood made a movie about him that won two Oscars.

His name was Melvin Dummar. He died in 2018. The old man in the desert, he always said, was Howard Hughes.

Was he a liar, or the unluckiest man in America?

text:
Sweden Built Its Own Defense Industry. Ukraine Should Pay Attention.

A bit off-topic from my usual crypto posts, but look at what Sweden has built with its own hands.

A country of roughly 10.5 million people produces fighter jets, submarines, artillery systems, missiles and advanced airborne surveillance aircraft. Its defense industry can compete in fields traditionally dominated by the United States and other major military powers.

Sweden is not a superpower. It does not have America's population, China's manufacturing scale or an unlimited defense budget.

Yet it developed capabilities that many much larger European countries allowed to disappear.

For Ukraine, this is worth studying. Not because our circumstances are identical, but because Sweden demonstrates what a relatively small country can achieve when defense production becomes a long-term national priority.

1. Neutrality does not mean depending on someone else

Sweden spent roughly two centuries outside formal military alliances before joining NATO in 2024. But its history of neutrality never meant that it could safely ignore the possibility of war.

The underlying calculation was straightforward: if you want to remain independent, you need the ability to defend that independence.

Sweden's geographical position reinforces this logic. Gotland, a large island in the Baltic Sea, has considerable strategic importance. Control of the island affects the ability to operate across the surrounding region and complicates military planning for anyone seeking dominance in the Baltic.

The wider lesson is not about one island. It is about the relationship between political independence and military capability.

A country may prefer peace, avoid unnecessary confrontation and have no intention of starting a war. None of those things guarantees that other states will leave it alone.

Europe is rediscovering this problem after decades of relying heavily on American security guarantees, Russian energy and global supply chains.

Sweden took a different approach: maintain the industrial knowledge required to build critical weapons at home.

That decision created options that cannot be purchased overnight.

2. Saab is the result of decades of industrial policy

Today, Saab is best known internationally for systems such as the Gripen fighter and GlobalEye airborne surveillance aircraft. Sweden also has expertise in submarines, artillery, engines and other defense technologies.

This capability did not appear because one company suddenly became exceptionally innovative.

Its foundations were laid in the 1930s, when growing tensions in Europe made Sweden reconsider the condition of its armed forces.

A central figure in the process was industrialist Marcus Wallenberg Jr., from one of Sweden's most influential business families. He believed that neutrality could not be sustained without the means to defend it.

The government pursued industrial consolidation rather than spreading scarce engineering talent and funding across numerous competing aircraft manufacturers.

In 1939, the merger of major aircraft businesses helped create Saab. The objective was not simply to establish another company. It was to build an industrial organization capable of delivering aircraft at the scale the country required.

The state also supported the export activity needed to help the industry grow.

After the Second World War, Sweden continued investing in research. Government-backed institutions worked on aerodynamics, radar, missile technology, radio systems, engines and other fields relevant to defense.

Even where Sweden imported finished technologies or components, domestic research remained important. The point was to retain the ability to understand, adapt and eventually improve systems rather than depend entirely on foreign suppliers.

That distinction matters.

Buying a weapon gives you a capability today. Developing the industrial and scientific base behind it gives you more control over what you can build tomorrow.

3. The Gripen reflects a particular way of thinking about war

The Saab JAS 39 Gripen is a fourth-generation multirole fighter that entered service in the 1990s.

Its significance is not limited to its performance in the air. The aircraft was designed around the practical constraints Sweden expected to face during a conflict.

A small country cannot assume that it will always have an unlimited supply of highly trained personnel, secure airbases or extensive maintenance infrastructure.

The Gripen's operating concept reflects that reality.

Its ground servicing was designed to be relatively quick and efficient. Under suitable conditions, preparing the aircraft for another mission can take around ten minutes with a small ground crew. Engine replacement was also designed to be much faster than on many conventional aircraft.

The aircraft can operate from relatively short stretches of road, rather than depending exclusively on large conventional airbases.

This matters because fixed infrastructure becomes a target during war.

If an enemy can destroy a limited number of airfields and effectively ground an entire air force, the defender has a serious vulnerability. Dispersed operations make that task more difficult.

The broader principle is simple: a weapon should not be judged only by its technical specifications.

You also need to ask:

How many people does it take to operate?
How quickly can it return to service?
How much specialist infrastructure does it require?
Can it keep functioning when conventional bases are damaged?
What does it cost to maintain over time?

A platform that looks impressive on paper but is difficult to sustain under combat conditions may be less useful than a system designed around the realities of the battlefield.

Sweden has spent decades treating those questions as part of the engineering problem.

4. Automation is a force multiplier when manpower is limited

Swedish artillery offers another example.

The Bandkanon 1, developed during the 1960s and now retired, was capable of firing 15 shells in 45 seconds. Its design emphasized a high rate of fire through an automated loading system.

The modern Archer self-propelled artillery system follows a different design, but the underlying principle remains relevant: automate as much of the process as practical and reduce the number of personnel exposed during operations.

Archer can be operated by a crew of three. Its automated systems handle much of the work that would otherwise require more manual intervention, and the crew can perform its tasks from within the protected cabin.

This is particularly important for Ukraine.

The country faces a war in which personnel are a finite resource. Mobilized soldiers cannot instantly replace years of technical experience, and every additional person required to operate a system creates another demand on recruitment, training and logistics.

Automation does not eliminate the need for skilled crews. It changes how much each crew can accomplish.

The same principle applies far beyond artillery. It affects air defense, reconnaissance, logistics, maintenance and command systems.

The objective is not to automate everything for its own sake. It is to reduce unnecessary workload, shorten the time between actions and allow smaller teams to operate effectively.

In a war of attrition, those advantages accumulate.

5. Cost is more than the purchase price

Swedish weapons are also designed with operational costs in mind.

The Gripen has often been marketed around comparatively economical maintenance and operating requirements. Figures commonly cited for its hourly flight cost are lower than estimates for some competing Western fighters, although direct comparisons depend heavily on what each calculation includes.

The important point is not to treat any single cost figure as universally definitive.

A fighter's real cost includes fuel, spare parts, maintenance personnel, training, infrastructure, availability and the time required to return damaged or serviced aircraft to operations.

A similar calculation applies to artillery and other equipment.

A system that needs fewer specialists, requires less support infrastructure and spends less time out of service may deliver more usable capability from the same budget.

For a country fighting a prolonged war, that can be as important as acquiring a technically superior platform.

The cheapest weapon is not necessarily the one with the lowest sticker price. It is the one that delivers the required capability at a sustainable total cost.

6. Sweden did not build this system in a single budget cycle

One of the most important parts of Sweden's experience is the relationship between government planning and industrial investment.

Defense companies cannot develop advanced aircraft, submarines or propulsion systems on the assumption that a customer might place an order next year.

These projects require long development periods, specialized employees, testing facilities, supply chains and expensive research. If demand disappears every time political priorities change, the skills and production capacity disappear with it.

Sweden addressed this problem through long-term defense planning and state support for research and development.

During the postwar period, domestic aircraft development remained a priority. Government commitments gave Saab a clearer basis for investing in successive aircraft programs, including the Tunnan, Draken and Viggen before the Gripen.

This created a cumulative advantage.

Each generation of aircraft depended on an ecosystem of engineers, suppliers, research institutions, manufacturing processes and operational experience. Knowledge from one program could inform the next.

That is how a country builds more than a product. It builds the capacity to produce the next product.

However, the Swedish model also had a less comfortable side.

Major defense decisions were historically shaped by close relationships among government officials, military leaders and industrial representatives. These arrangements helped maintain continuity, but they also raised serious questions about transparency and conflicts of interest.

The lesson is not that defense spending should be shielded from public scrutiny.

It is that long-term planning and accountability have to coexist. Without continuity, industrial capabilities can collapse. Without oversight, concentrated influence can lead to waste, favoritism or decisions that serve private interests rather than national security.

A sustainable system needs both.

7. The end of the Cold War exposed the danger of losing capacity

When the Cold War ended, Sweden reduced defense spending. Its industrial sector also became more dependent on foreign components and ownership.

Several important businesses moved into the hands of larger international defense groups. Bofors, for example, became part of BAE Systems. The former Volvo Aero engine business was acquired by an American company, while Sweden's submarine-building capability came under German ownership.

Saab remained the central Swedish defense company, but the wider industrial ecosystem had changed.

This is a familiar pattern across Europe.

When the immediate threat appears to fade, governments look for savings. Domestic production can seem unnecessarily expensive when a foreign supplier offers an existing product. Research budgets are reduced, production lines close and specialists move into other industries.

At first, the consequences may not be obvious. The country can continue buying equipment from abroad.

The problem becomes visible when demand suddenly rises or the supplier's own government prioritizes its domestic armed forces.

Industrial capacity cannot be switched on like a light.

A closed production line, dispersed workforce or lost engineering team may take years to rebuild. In some cases, the knowledge has disappeared so thoroughly that restarting production becomes a new development project.

Sweden's post-Cold War experience shows that even a country with a strong defense tradition can lose parts of its independence if it assumes the strategic environment has permanently changed.

8. Russia's invasion of Ukraine changed the calculation

Russia's 2014 attack on Ukraine forced Sweden to reassess its security assumptions.

The country reversed its decision to sell its submarine manufacturing business to Germany and returned that capability to Saab's management. It also restored conscription in 2018, after suspending it in 2010.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 made the broader problem impossible for much of Europe to ignore.

A military threat that had seemed distant became a direct question of readiness, ammunition stocks, production rates and the ability to sustain a prolonged conflict.

Sweden's experience illustrates the value of reacting before every consequence becomes unavoidable.

The country had not maintained every capability at its Cold War peak. It had cut spending and accepted greater foreign dependence in some areas. But it still retained a domestic industrial base and the institutional knowledge needed to rebuild parts of its defense posture.

That starting position matters.

A country that has kept its engineers, research institutions and production experience has more options than one that must reconstruct the entire ecosystem from scratch.

9. What Ukraine can learn from Sweden

Ukraine's circumstances are different. We face an active, large-scale war against a neighboring aggressor, while Sweden developed much of its industry under different strategic conditions.

But several lessons are directly relevant.

First, treat defense production as a long-term national capability.

A defense industry cannot be built around emergency purchases alone. Ukraine needs predictable demand, stable multi-year programs and financing that allows companies to invest in people, equipment and research.

Second, design for the personnel actually available.

Equipment should be evaluated by how effectively small teams can operate and maintain it. Automation, repairability, ease of training and reduced maintenance requirements are not secondary conveniences. They affect combat capacity.

Third, build around the conditions of the battlefield.

Dispersed operations, damaged infrastructure, difficult weather and disrupted supply chains should be considered from the beginning. Systems that remain useful under these conditions are more valuable than equipment that depends on an ideal operating environment.

Fourth, protect technical knowledge.

Ukraine needs more than factories assembling imported components. Domestic expertise in electronics, engines, software, sensors, materials, propulsion and system integration creates the foundation for future generations of weapons.

Foreign technology and partnerships can accelerate development, but the country should understand which capabilities it cannot afford to lose.

Fifth, maintain continuity without abandoning oversight.

Long-term programs need to survive political changes, but stable funding must not become a blank check. Procurement should be subject to meaningful controls, clear responsibilities and scrutiny designed to prevent corruption without making essential decisions impossible.

Sixth, think about the entire production ecosystem.

A modern weapon depends on suppliers, testing, maintenance, training, research and access to components. Supporting one flagship company is not enough if the wider supply chain remains fragile.

And finally, do not confuse the absence of immediate danger with the absence of a need to prepare.

10. The real advantage is the ability to keep building

Sweden's defense industry is not the product of one aircraft, one company or one unusually successful procurement decision.

It emerged from decades of investment in research, industrial coordination, manufacturing experience and the willingness to maintain capabilities that might not always look economical in peacetime.

The country also made mistakes. It reduced spending after the Cold War and allowed important parts of its industrial base to become foreign-owned. Rebuilding readiness has required new decisions and renewed investment.

That makes the Swedish example more useful, not less. It shows both what sustained planning can achieve and what can be lost when a country assumes the strategic environment will remain favorable.

Ukraine does not need to copy Sweden's model in every detail. Our geography, threat level, workforce and industrial base are different.

But the central principle is worth keeping:

A country is more secure when it can develop, adapt, repair and produce the systems its armed forces need — instead of relying entirely on someone else's capacity.

Alliances matter. Foreign assistance matters. Imported weapons matter.

But domestic industrial knowledge gives a country more control over its own future.

For Sweden, this principle shaped defense planning long before the current security crisis in Europe. For Ukraine, the full-scale invasion has made the cost of dependence painfully clear.

The next challenge is to turn that lesson into an industrial strategy that lasts beyond the emergency — and to build capabilities that will still be there when the next crisis arrives.
